## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{100}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why is a completed agent run not enough evidence to justify a release?_

A runtime that enforces budgets, survives crashes, and recovers from bad actions still cannot say whether the task got done. An agent can report success after weakening the test that would have caught its bug, finish a targeted check while leaving a required regression test unrun, or pass once and fail the same task on the next trial. Activity counters miss these distinctions. Evaluation makes completion criteria explicit and connects each verdict to the evidence that supports it. Comparing systems also requires comparable tasks and enough observations to distinguish a useful change from variation; diagnosing a failure requires more than finding an adjacent error in a trace. Without that discipline, teams can release a regression or train on trajectories whose apparent success reflects a gap in the checks. Through the H·S·A lens, evaluation examines the results supported by state evidence, the resources consumed across the horizon, and the authority exercised along the way.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Define task acceptance from scoped outcome, process, resource, and residual-duty criteria while preserving incomplete verdicts
- Design comparable task fixtures and a grading boundary that accounts for untrusted candidate artifacts
- Select and calibrate outcome checks, process assessments, and human or model judgments for declared criteria
- Compare stochastic systems using explicit sampling units, uncertainty, paired outcomes, and matched-budget metrics
- Construct useful trajectory traces and retention policies with stated capture, sampling, and privacy limits
- Diagnose failures through recorded evidence and controlled interventions without overstating causal conclusions
- Design staged releases that combine comparative evidence with bounded exposure and explicit stopping rules
- Assemble an evaluation record that justifies a scoped decision and preserves the evidence needed for later curation

:::

## The Task Acceptance Contract {#sec-vol3-evaluation-contract}

The connection-pool repair has reached several milestones. Its runtime can reconstruct candidate `ws_r18`, retain the unresolved `test_r18` operation, and account for a temporary integration-test environment. A targeted test result supports that candidate and that check; a completed cleanup supports the cleanup postcondition. Whether the whole repair meets its requirements is a separate question. @Sec-vol3-sagas-case-study ended with a fault-test plan that kept those outcomes apart, and evaluation now specifies which evidence counts toward accepting the task.

Consider a declared evaluation trial of the same repair problem. The task identifier is `pool_repair_01`, the initial fixture is `pool_fixture_v1`, and the acceptance criteria have version `repair_accept_v1`. The evaluated system configuration, `candidate_v2`, names the selected model, prompt, tools, and harness configuration; it names a system, not a source revision. Trial `eval_pool_01_candidate_v2_run1` produces a new candidate artifact, `ws_r19`, whose checks must refer to those exact bytes. A recovered result for `ws_r18` remains evidence about `ws_r18` only.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_hsa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes, Horizon, State, and Authority, highlighted."}

*Evaluation examines the state a result rests on, the resources spent across its horizon, and the authority it exercised.*
:::

A **trial**\index{Evaluation trial!definition} is one execution under the declared task, fixture, system configuration, and evaluation protocol. A second execution receives another trial identity even if those inputs are unchanged. Comparing `candidate_v2` with `baseline_v1` requires comparable trials under both system configurations. Repeating this one repair yields more trials of one task, not more tasks, and @sec-vol3-evaluation-resampling separates the two sources of variation. First, every trial needs an explicit acceptance rule.

### Separate evidence dimensions from a pass sequence

The task contract specifies required outcomes, permitted actions, resource limits, and the evidence needed to assess them. An evaluation contract makes those criteria operational: what is checked, on which version, by which instrument, at what observation boundary, and with what treatment of unavailable evidence. @Tbl-vol3-eval-contract-hierarchy separates four dimensions of evidence. They are parallel records, not a sequence in which an early error voids later evidence.

| Dimension             | Evidence to inspect                                                                                                                    | Consequence for the repair                                                                                     |
|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Proposal validity     | Completed proposal, parsing and schema results, represented tool and arguments                                                         | An invalid configuration rejected before dispatch can be repaired; the rejection alone need not fail the trial |
| Execution behavior    | Admitted operations and attempts, endpoint outcomes, ordering, observed partial effects, and recovery history                          | An accepted request is not necessarily a finished test; a timeout can leave an operation unresolved            |
| Task outcome          | Exact candidate artifact, required defect and regression checks, final answer, and any declared qualitative rubric                     | A targeted pass supports only its coverage; a readable report cannot replace missing required checks           |
| Constraint compliance | Authority decisions and observed effects, protected-artifact checks, consumption and liability, elapsed intervals, and residual owners | Good final code does not erase a prohibited effect or satisfy an unmet cleanup or budget condition             |

: **Dimensions of Task Evaluation**: Each dimension contributes scoped evidence. The task's declared criteria determine which findings reject a trial, which remain pending, and which serve only as diagnostics. {#tbl-vol3-eval-contract-hierarchy}

A proposal with the wrong argument type can be rejected locally, corrected, and followed by a successful repair; a task that permits such recovery still accepts the trial. A policy that forbids even proposing a particular disclosure makes that attempt a failing criterion instead. The record therefore states whether each event was a proposal, an admitted request, or an observed effect, because the three support different findings.

The separation keeps diagnostic value after acceptance is already lost. When a required protected-file condition fails, the candidate's test results, elapsed time, and cleanup still explain the failure and guide the repair, although they cannot override the failed condition.

::: {#dfn-vol3-accepted-task .callout-definition title="Accepted task"}

***Accepted task***\index{Accepted task!definition} is a task completion credited to a particular trial because the available evidence satisfies its declared outcome, process, resource, and residual-duty criteria at the required evidence level.

1. **Significance**: Acceptance is the denominator of cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}}$ in @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task. Every rejected or unresolved trial's spend is charged to the accepted ones, so a looser acceptance rule lowers the reported cost without making the system cheaper.
2. **Distinction**: Passing one verifier is narrower than acceptance when other required checks, constraints, or duties remain. The task identity is distinct from the trial that attempts it.
3. **Common pitfall**: Crediting a trial from a model's completion claim, a transport status, or a test result for a different candidate revision.

:::

### State what each instrument establishes

Three sources of evidence have different limits. Runtime guards and external checks are the two halves of invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}), with mechanical bounds enforced below the model and evidence about the result gathered above it. Runtime guards enforce bounds at the boundaries they mediate, such as withholding an unauthorized dispatch. External checks assess specified properties, such as whether the submitted candidate passes a defect reproducer and the required regression suite. Human or model judgments assess a declared rubric, such as whether the final report accurately explains its evidence and limitations. A rubric can be a required acceptance criterion, and its judgment then needs the calibration developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-grading.

Protecting a grader from agent modification secures the integrity of its measurement; coverage is a separate property. A test suite can miss a defect, and a candidate artifact can contain code that attacks the process executing its tests, which the grading boundary of the next section addresses. The rule from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-continuations applies throughout: a check establishes exactly the properties its coverage and assumptions support.

::: {#dfn-state-delta-verification .callout-definition title="State-delta verification"}

***State-delta verification***\index{State-delta verification!definition} checks specified properties of an observed change between declared initial and resulting environment states, using measurements tied to the relevant versions and task criteria.

1. **Significance**: It can distinguish a claimed repair from an observed artifact or service change that meets the selected checks.
2. **Distinction**: The change is a defined comparison, not literal subtraction of arbitrary filesystem trees or databases and not proof of every aspect of correctness.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating any nonempty patch or successful tool response as evidence that the intended change occurred without an unwanted one.

:::

The criterion selects the observation and the instrument. A read-only analysis succeeds by returning an answer supported by the required sources and rubric within its access and disclosure constraints, with no persistent state change. A repair can require history as well as final files, since an unauthorized deletion followed by restoration still violates a policy that forbids the deletion.

Resource evidence needs named boundaries too. Ordinary execution and finalization are measured against their separately declared allowances from @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting, and elapsed time runs between specified timestamps, so overlapping model and tool intervals are never summed as wall-clock duration. Tokens, money, and occupied resources stay separate quantities. Settled charges also stay separate from outstanding reserved liability, which an evaluation cutoff neither refunds nor stops.

### Preserve mixed and incomplete verdicts

For each required criterion, retain its result and supporting evidence. Use `pass` when that evidence meets the criterion, `fail` when it establishes a violation, `pending` while a required assessment or outcome is still expected within the observation window, and `unknown` when the necessary evidence is insufficient or unavailable at the cutoff. Record why an unknown arose. These are evaluation verdicts, not new trajectory lifecycle states.

Under a contract that requires every mandatory criterion, an established failure makes the overall verdict `fail` even if other criteria remain unresolved. If all required criteria pass with adequate evidence, the trial is accepted. Otherwise it remains pending or unknown under the declared observation policy. A binary comparison needs an explicit rule for incomplete cases, because dropping them changes the population being measured.

::: {#exmp-13-repair-acceptance-record .callout-example title="A targeted pass is not a completed evaluation"}

**Problem**: Trial `eval_pool_01_candidate_v2_run1` submits `ws_r19` under `repair_accept_v1`. The contract requires the defect reproducer and designated regression checks to pass, the report to state the supported scope, permitted actions and resource allowances to hold, and temporary resources to be released or transferred under its residual-duty policy. At an interim observation, can this trial be accepted?

| Required evidence               | Observation for this trial                                                                                                                  | Verdict at this observation                                        |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Candidate-specific defect check | The designated reproducer passed on `ws_r19`                                                                                                | `pass` for this check only                                         |
| Required regression coverage    | The designated suite has not yet produced a complete result                                                                                 | `pending`                                                          |
| Report scope                    | The declared review found that the report identifies the candidate, completed check, and missing coverage                                   | `pass` under that rubric and review                                |
| Permitted process               | Retained mediation and protected-artifact checks satisfy the specified process criteria; a malformed proposal was corrected before dispatch | `pass` within the stated coverage                                  |
| Resource criteria               | Admissions remained within the configured bounds, but required final usage evidence for an outstanding operation is not yet available       | Admission-bound check `pass`; final-accounting criterion `pending` |
| Residual duties                 | The designated service acknowledged ownership of the remaining operation and charge reconciliation, as this contract permits                | Handoff criterion `pass`; the external outcome remains unresolved  |

: **An Interim Repair Evaluation Record**: Hypothetical findings for one identified trial. Each result retains its criterion and scope; successful handoff does not establish the result of the transferred operation. {#tbl-vol3-repair-acceptance-record}

**Result**: The trial in @tbl-vol3-repair-acceptance-record is not yet accepted. Its overall verdict is `pending` because required regression and accounting evidence is still expected. If the regression suite reports a required check failure, the overall verdict becomes `fail`, while the unresolved charge remains recorded. If the observation window closes first, the affected criteria become `unknown`, a gap that neither the targeted pass nor the accepted handoff fills. Later evidence can update the evaluation record without reviving an obsolete continuation or erasing the earlier verdict.

**Systems insight**: The record distinguishes task completion, successful runtime enforcement, grader coverage, and owned residual work. A favorable result in one category cannot substitute for missing evidence in another.

:::

The acceptance contract now states what the trial must establish and what its verdict means. Its usefulness in a comparison still depends on the conditions under which the evidence was obtained. A different starting repository, changed dependency, or exposed grading solution can change the score without improving the agent system. Comparable fixtures and a protected grading boundary make that next distinction possible.

## Hermetic Evaluation Gyms {#sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms}

The repair trial produces candidate artifact `ws_r19`. To compare `candidate_v2` with `baseline_v1`, the evaluator needs more than two final reports. Both systems must encounter the declared task under comparable starting conditions, and each result must be checked against the artifact that its trial actually produced. If one run inherits a repaired file, a changed dependency, or a still-running test from another, the observed difference no longer isolates the intended system change.

An **evaluation gym**\index{Evaluation gym!definition} provides the task's interactive environment, controlled starting conditions, and interfaces for collecting evaluation evidence. Its **hermetic boundary**\index{Hermetic boundary!definition} specifies which dependencies are supplied or controlled and which external interactions are excluded. The boundary is an experimental contract. It fixes the declared conditions, and a stochastic environment qualifies once its variation and sampling policy are declared; identical model responses and complete production fidelity are outside the promise.

### Specify the fixture before running the trial

A **task fixture**\index{Task fixture!definition} packages the initial state and dependencies needed to instantiate an evaluation task. For the connection-pool repair, `pool_fixture_v1` identifies the starting repository, dependency versions, test-service behavior, and permitted task data. The fixture supplies the conditions under which the system attempts the task; the separate acceptance criteria specify how its result will be judged.

@Tbl-vol3-evaluation-fixture-contract records the conditions that must accompany the trial. Stable identifiers make the record referable; accessible versioned contents make it usable.

| Fixture component       | What the repair evaluation declares                                                                                            | Why the comparison needs it                                          |
|:------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Initial task state      | Starting source revision, supplied defect description, permitted files and any initial service state                           | Neither system inherits another trial's fix or an undeclared hint    |
| Executable dependencies | Toolchain, packages, tool interfaces, service fixtures, and relevant configuration versions                                    | A dependency change is not mistaken for a system improvement         |
| Interaction policy      | Available tools, permitted data and destinations, resource limits, and external behaviors represented                          | Both systems face the declared task and authority boundary           |
| Variation policy        | Fixed or sampled fault conditions, scheduling and random inputs where controlled, and recorded provenance where not controlled | The experiment distinguishes intended variation from missing control |
| Evidence boundary       | Exported candidate identity, protected grader configuration, criteria version, and allowed development feedback                | A result applies to the actual submitted artifact and check          |
| Trial lifecycle         | Reset readiness, output capture, observation cutoff, cleanup and residual ownership                                            | Late work and retained state cannot silently enter the next trial    |

: **A fixture contract for comparable trials**: The manifest defines what is held fixed, what may vary, and what evidence is retained. It does not assert that every production condition is represented. {#tbl-vol3-evaluation-fixture-contract}

The comparison also declares how tasks are selected, since repeated trials of one fixture characterize only that repair (@sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor). A fixed model seed leaves serving internals and observation order free, so the record states the available provenance and the remaining variability.

### Control interactions without hiding the behavior being tested

Interactive evaluation measures the loop: the system can inspect the repository, receive diagnostics, revise a candidate, and request checks. A static answer test measures a component and leaves those interactions unexercised. The gym supplies the behaviors that the declared task and claim require.

A document-analysis fixture might pin the supplied files and retrieval collection while grading a read-only answer. A browser-task fixture might also specify account permissions and initial application state. Both grade outputs other than a patch, because the fixture follows the task's interactions and criteria rather than the repair's toolchain.

Real tools in an isolated fixture can exercise compilation, filesystem changes, and test execution. Stateful service emulators can represent operations whose later responses depend on earlier actions. Recorded responses can support a narrower replay boundary when the request, arguments, versions, and required ordering match. As @sec-vol3-persistence-replay established, a changed request cannot simply receive the next historical response. The evaluator must supply behavior valid for the changed path or report the fixture's unsupported interaction.

For the repair's temporary environment, a service fixture that always returns immediate provisioning success cannot test recovery from a lost reply or delayed creation. A fault fixture instead controls whether the request reached the endpoint, when its effect occurred, and which acknowledgment was withheld, which makes the uncertainty from @sec-vol3-sagas-case-study observable inside the fixture. Evaluation against real external services needs its own authorized scope and effect accounting; labeling a run a benchmark grants no authority.

Deterministic mocks improve control but can omit contention, timing, partial effects, or unusual error responses. More realistic services introduce setup cost and variability. Choose fidelity around the claim: a configuration-validation test needs different behavior from an experiment about retry safety. Report omitted behaviors with the score, since a high score on a simplified fixture is evidence only for the conditions it represents.

### Reset the state relevant to the experiment

The reset contract in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset supplies the execution boundary. Evaluation adds the requirement that each admitted trial begins in conditions compatible with its fixture. Stop or account for owned writers, capture the candidate consistently, retire the old trial's usable authority, and reset the mutable resources that the next trial could inherit. A clean repository still leaves any background job, host-side request queue, or stateful mock service to reset.

An unresolved previous operation keeps its identity and owner, and a resource that delayed work can still affect stays out of the pool. A replacement fixture proceeds independently when the isolation contract establishes that separation; discarding the old workspace leaves the earlier operation unsettled. Reset readiness and the previous trial's final verdict are separate records.

Copy-on-write or prepared snapshots can reduce repeated initialization under the reset contract. Measure preparation, reset, grading, queueing, and task execution separately when reporting evaluation throughput. The quantity that matters is the time until a trial can begin, which a fast lease allocation can understate.

Declared sharing is compatible with a valid experiment. Immutable dependencies can be shared under the containment contract, and a warmed cache is an intentional condition when measuring warm operation, while a cold-start comparison needs a different policy. Resource contention and trial order matter when they influence the measured endpoint. State those conditions or randomize assignment, so that an uncontrolled difference is never attributed to the candidate configuration.

### Protect the grader from the submitted code

Visible development tests give the system useful feedback. Held-out acceptance tests, the sealed tests among the closure evidence levels of @sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure, serve a different purpose: they assess the submitted artifact without exposing their complete specification as another optimization target. Keep reference solutions, protected test definitions, grading configuration, and the authoritative result store outside the agent's accessible task environment. Capture `ws_r19` at a consistent boundary and bind the grading result to those exact bytes and versions. Grading a workspace while it continues to change would break that binding.

Submitted code stays untrusted after the agent process stops. If a clean grader imports the candidate package into the same interpreter as its assertions, that code can alter shared objects or the test runner. If hidden tests are mounted where candidate code can read them during execution, their confidentiality is gone, wherever they sat during the agent's run. Read-only files prevent direct edits and nothing more.

The grader design must therefore specify both boundaries: the live agent's access and the submitted artifact's execution reach. A trusted controller can select tests and collect measurements through a constrained interface while candidate code executes in a separately limited environment. Protect the controller's decision logic and result storage, restrict candidate-supplied configuration and executable hooks according to the task's patch-admission policy, which names the protected files and permitted edits, and treat candidate-produced logs as untrusted observations rather than authoritative verdicts. The actual test inputs sent to a candidate may become visible to it; hiding the entire suite is a different promise. @Fig-vol3-eval-gym-architecture places the trial's sandbox and this grading boundary side by side.

::: {#fig-vol3-eval-gym-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Trial Sandbox and Grading Boundary**: The agent under test edits and runs checks inside a single-use fixture whose base image is shared read-only and whose writes land in a per-trial copy-on-write layer; external egress is blocked, and service fixtures stand in for the dependencies the task declares. The captured candidate `ws_r19` crosses to a grading boundary, where a trusted controller keeps the held-out tests, criteria, and result store and sends selected tests to a separately limited execution of the candidate code. That execution remains the attack surface, because submitted code runs with the tests it receives, so its outputs are untrusted observations until the controller binds each criterion's verdict to the exact artifact." fig-alt="Two regions. Left, a task sandbox with an agent-under-test box labeled with configuration candidate_v2, an arrow labeled edits and runs checks into a fixture box holding a read-only shared base image and a copy-on-write layer for the trial's writes, and an interaction boundary box with external egress blocked and service fixtures. An arrow carries the captured artifact ws_r19, exact bytes, to the right region, a grading boundary. There a trusted controller holding held-out tests, criteria repair_accept_v1, decision logic, and the result store sends selected tests down to a dashed candidate execution box marked attack surface, which returns untrusted outputs and logs. The controller also feeds a criterion-level verdicts box listing pass, fail, pending, and unknown, bound to ws_r19."}
![](images/svg/ch13-eval-gym-architecture.svg)
:::

Some repository tests require in-process execution with the submitted code, and such a harness states that attack surface and assesses it. Adversarial fixture checks test known ways to read protected material, change the runner, or forge reported outcomes, and passing them supports the covered boundary.

When grading fails to produce required evidence, the check keeps an unavailable or pending status, and the acceptance policy decides whether a declared condition, such as a timeout, counts as a failure.

### Keep development feedback separate from evaluation evidence

Leakage can enter before or during a trial. Training data may overlap a public benchmark; a retrieval index may expose a reference solution; prior trial memory may carry a held-out answer into the next run. Development feedback is legitimate only within the declared protocol. Repeatedly tuning prompts against held-out failures changes that set's role from independent assessment toward development data.

Track the provenance and allowed use of task descriptions, solutions, tests, and derived traces. Check accessible retrieval sources and retained memories as well as the local workspace. Similarity and deduplication tools flag overlap for investigation; falling below their threshold is no proof that two tasks are independent. Private or newly created tasks close some exposure routes, and @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation develops the corresponding training-split discipline.

One benchmark shows the connection between fixtures and criteria. SWE-bench presents repository issues and evaluates generated patches against task-specific tests [@jimenez2024swebench]. Its [evaluation procedure](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.06770v3#A4) checks both tests expected to change from failing to passing and tests expected to remain passing. This grounds “repair” in behavior on a specified repository state, with the coverage of those tests as the limit of the claim.

Two other benchmarks show different verification regimes. GAIA poses questions with one short, unambiguous answer and grades the normalized final answer by exact match [@mialon2023gaia], so the checker is cheap and exact for that property but observes nothing about the actions taken to reach it. WebArena hosts self-contained web applications and grades many tasks by querying the resulting application state rather than the agent's transcript [@zhou2024webarena]. A state assertion checks only the records it queries. An unrelated order deleted on the way to a correct result passes unless the acceptance contract also checks for unintended mutations, which is why the constraint-compliance dimension in @tbl-vol3-eval-contract-hierarchy needs its own evidence.

::: {.callout-checkpoint title="Comparable trials and protected evidence"}

- [ ] **Identity**: Why must a result for `ws_r18` not become the grade for newly submitted `ws_r19`, even on the same task fixture?
- [ ] **Fidelity**: Which recovery claim cannot be tested by a provisioning mock that always returns immediate success?
- [ ] **Grader boundary**: Hidden tests are absent during the agent's run but share an interpreter with candidate code during grading. Which attack surface remains, and which change to the grader design closes it?
- [ ] **Reset**: A previous trial left an unresolved remote job. Would you return its sandbox to the pool, and what must be established first?
- [ ] **Leakage**: Why can repeated tuning on held-out errors weaken the evaluation even when every sandbox resets correctly?

:::

The fixture now supplies comparable interactions and a stated boundary for collecting evidence. That evidence still needs interpretation: which checks establish each acceptance criterion, which process properties matter, and where a fallible judgment is required. Grading makes those choices explicit.

## Grading Trajectories {#sec-vol3-evaluation-grading}

Two trials of `pool_repair_01` can submit byte-identical source files and still differ in acceptance status. For `ws_r19`, only the targeted check has passed, while another trial of the same patch may already have established the regression and accounting evidence that `ws_r19` still awaits. Comparing the patches alone cannot tell the two apart. Grading connects each declared criterion to evidence, records what that evidence establishes, and preserves what remains unknown.

### Outcome and process criteria

An outcome criterion concerns the requested result, such as the specified regression checks against `ws_r19` or a read-only answer's accuracy and coverage. An outcome check may still inspect history when history determines the result, because a final resource count alone cannot establish that no duplicate allocation occurred.

Process criteria concern how the trial reached its result. The evidence that process deserves separate grading comes from reasoning tasks. On math word problems, Uesato et al. [-@uesato2022solving] found that outcome and process supervision reached similar final-answer accuracy while process supervision sharply reduced correct answers reached through flawed reasoning, and Lightman et al. [-@lightman2023let] found that process-supervised reward models selected correct solutions more reliably; @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification develops those verifiers. For an agent, the process also includes actions. Current authority, forbidden disclosures, required approvals, and recovery obligations can be mandatory conditions of acceptance. Other process measurements diagnose behavior without deciding acceptance by themselves. Tool-call validity measures the fraction of proposed calls that satisfy their schemas, which is silent on whether the chosen calls were useful.

Either kind of criterion can be assessed by a mechanical check, human review, or model judgment. A test runner supplies evidence only for the checks it executed, and a resource-status query only under its endpoint's semantics, so each result is bound to the trial and artifact it assessed.

Diagnostic metrics need their own denominators and endpoints. A recovery rate should count episodes that achieved a stated recovery condition among the eligible episodes observed, while reporting unresolved episodes and the observation cutoff separately; a different next action alone is not a recovery. Partial-credit scores show which checked subgoals were met and leave a failed mandatory condition failed. Report turns, tokens, and costs with the task outcomes rather than treating a shorter failed trial as an efficiency improvement.

### Measure grader errors against an independent assessment

A check can reject satisfactory work or accept unsatisfactory work. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) separates checking a stated property from establishing that the property captures the task, so a grader's error rates must be measured rather than assumed from its repeatability. False acceptance is especially consequential when accepted trajectories support release or later training, but the two error directions answer different questions. Let $F$ denote failure of the specified criterion under an independent reference assessment, and let $\mathrm{Acc}$ denote acceptance by the grader under study. Then distinguish

$$\text{False-acceptance rate}=P(\mathrm{Acc}\mid F), \qquad
\text{Failure among accepted}=P(F\mid \mathrm{Acc}).$$

The **false-acceptance rate**\index{False-acceptance rate!definition} conditions on reference-assessed failures and measures how often the grader accepted them. Failure among accepted conditions on grader acceptances and measures how often independent assessment found failure among them. A random audit of accepted outputs estimates the second quantity; the first requires reference-assessed failures, including those the grader rejected. Both need stated sampling, enough assessed cases, and an uncertainty estimate.

The distinction matters when the system changes, because failure among accepted cases depends on the prevalence and kinds of failures as well as on the grader's errors. A candidate can expose gaps that were rare in the calibration set, so each candidate's audit checks whether the relevant failure types and grader errors changed. Comparing the size of a score gain with a historical false-acceptance rate settles neither question.

Construct calibration cases from the intended task population, with deliberate coverage of important failure modes, and assess the relevant artifacts and observations independently against the same versioned rubric. Reference assessors also err and disagree, so the calibration set keeps its adjudication procedure and unresolved labels. A set that oversamples failures reports that design, since its unweighted error fraction among accepted cases describes the calibration mix rather than deployment. Held-out assessment cases stay separate from cases used to tune the grader.

### Calibrate qualitative judgment

A report's adequacy or a repair explanation's clarity may require judgment rather than an exact test. A **large language model (LLM) judge**\index{LLM judge!definition} is a model used to score such criteria under a rubric. The evaluation contract states whether its verdict is a required qualitative criterion, a signal for human review, or a diagnostic score. A favorable judgment cannot override another required criterion's failure or turn unavailable evidence into a pass.

Ground the judge in authorized evidence and discrete rubric items. For the repair explanation, those items can distinguish describing the patch accurately, identifying which checks ran, and acknowledging unresolved work. Supply the relevant trusted result records rather than relying solely on the candidate's summary. A tool-assisted judge inherits the same authority and disclosure boundaries as any other tool user. Candidate text and artifacts remain untrusted inputs to the grader, not instructions that may revise its rubric.

Zheng et al. [-@zheng2023judging] measured position and verbosity biases in model judges and found the evidence for self-enhancement bias inconclusive, so each judge is tested on its own workload. For pairwise judging, declare order swapping, ties, inconsistent decisions, and abstentions before scoring, and keep their counts in the denominator; discarding inconvenient comparisons changes the population being reported. A judge from a different model family is not independent by that fact alone.

For categorical ratings of the same cases, Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960] summarizes agreement relative to the raters' marginal label frequencies:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

Here $p_o$ is the observed agreement fraction, and $p_e=\sum_y p_{y,1}p_{y,2}$ uses each rater's fraction of labels in category $y$. When $p_e=1$, the expression is undefined. High raw agreement can arise from heavily concentrated label frequencies.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-kappa-chance
#| echo: false
# CHANCE AGREEMENT UNDER A CONCENTRATED BASE RATE (LEGO)
# Goal: Show raw agreement produced with zero agreement beyond chance.
# Scope: Two raters labeling "pass" independently of the case, same marginal rate.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_percent, check

class KappaChance:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical marginal pass rate shared by both raters.
    pass_rate = 0.90
    chk_rate = 0.80  # checkpoint exercise: a second hypothetical marginal rate

    # 2. EXECUTE: independence makes observed agreement equal chance agreement.
    p_o = pass_rate**2 + (1 - pass_rate) ** 2
    p_e = pass_rate * pass_rate + (1 - pass_rate) * (1 - pass_rate)
    kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)

    # 3. GUARD: textbook arithmetic.
    check(abs(p_o - 0.82) < 1e-12, "Raw agreement from chance alone")
    check(abs(kappa) < 1e-12, "No agreement beyond chance")
    check(0.5 < chk_rate < pass_rate, "Checkpoint rate differs from the worked rate")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    pass_rate_str = fmt_percent(pass_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    chk_rate_str = fmt_percent(chk_rate, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_o_str = fmt_percent(p_o, precision=0, style="prose")
    kappa_str = fmt(kappa, precision=0)
```

If two raters each label `{python} KappaChance.pass_rate_str` of cases as passing, independently of what the case contains, they agree on `{python} KappaChance.p_o_str` of cases by chance alone and $\kappa$ is `{python} KappaChance.kappa_str`. Report those frequencies, disagreements, and assessment coverage with kappa; the coefficient measures agreement, not whether either rater is correct.

Select a grader's operating policy using the errors that matter for its declared role. Review disagreement cases, report uncertainty for the relevant error estimates, and recalibrate when the rubric, judge, evidence interface, or evaluated population changes, because shared mistakes survive high agreement.

::: {.callout-checkpoint title="Defend a grading verdict"}

- [ ] **Evidence scope**: The trial's targeted check passes on `ws_r19`, but required regression and accounting evidence remain pending under `repair_accept_v1`. Which criteria are supported, and why does an acknowledged residual-duty handoff not fill those gaps?
- [ ] **Conditional denominator**: An audit samples only grader-accepted reports. Does its failure fraction estimate $P(\mathrm{Acc}\mid F)$ or $P(F\mid \mathrm{Acc})$? What population is missing for the other estimate?
- [ ] **Process requirement**: When can a recovered malformed proposal remain a diagnostic event, and when must a process violation reject the trial despite a correct final artifact?
- [ ] **Agreement vs. truth**: Two judges each pass `{python} KappaChance.chk_rate_str` of reports, independently of what the reports contain. Estimate their raw agreement and $\kappa$, and decide whether that agreement supports using either one as an acceptance grader.

:::

Grading yields criterion-level verdicts, their evidence and limitations, and diagnostic measurements for the observed trials. Generalizing beyond those trials is a statistical question: @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor separates task and run variation and compares baseline and candidate systems on paired outcomes.

## Statistical Evaluation Rigor {#sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor}

Suppose `candidate_v2` accepts a few more sampled tasks than `baseline_v1` in one sweep. That gain can be noise, while a smaller gain can be informative when the comparison preserves which tasks changed outcome. Deciding which requires naming the population the result should describe and accounting for variation in both the tasks and their executions. The uncertainty that matters therefore belongs to the comparison rather than to each system's separate score.

### Distinguish tasks from repeated runs {#sec-vol3-evaluation-resampling}

A task identifies a problem and its declared fixture and criteria. A run is one execution of a system configuration on that task. The connection-pool repair supplies one such task, and another artifact for it is another run of the same task. Model sampling and permitted environmental variation produce different outcomes on repeated runs, even at a fixed seed or temperature (@sec-vol3-persistence-replay).

Let $p_i$ be a fixed system's probability of acceptance on task $i$ under the declared execution and grading protocol. Suppose tasks are independently sampled from a specified population, and $R$ runs are independent conditional on each task. For the mean across $N$ tasks with the same number of runs per task,

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat p)=\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}}{N}+\frac{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}}{NR},\qquad
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}=\operatorname{Var}(p_i),\quad
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}=\mathbb E[p_i(1-p_i)].$$ {#eq-variance-decomposition}

The first term in @eq-variance-decomposition reflects task difficulty; the second reflects execution variation within a task. More repeats shrink only the second term, while more independently sampled tasks shrink both. Once $R$ exceeds $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}/\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}$, the run term is already the smaller one, and the next unit of evaluation budget buys more precision as new tasks than as repeats.

A fixed benchmark suite supports a different target: mean performance on those particular tasks. Repeated runs can estimate that target more precisely without making the suite representative of future work. Related tasks from one repository, shared service outages, or cross-trial state leakage can also violate independent-task assumptions. Preserve the relevant clusters in the sampling and analysis. Counting every run as an independent new task would overstate the information collected.

### Estimate one acceptance probability {#sec-vol3-evaluation-wilson}

For one run on each independently sampled task under a fixed protocol, let $X$ of $N$ trials be accepted. The binomial model estimates the population acceptance probability by $\hat p=X/N$. A confidence interval expresses uncertainty from this sampling model only; grader error, missing outcomes, contamination, and a changed task distribution need their own accounting.

The familiar Wald interval,

$$\hat p\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{N}},$$

can perform poorly near the boundaries and collapses to zero width when all observed outcomes agree. The **Wilson score interval**\index{Wilson score interval!definition} avoids that degeneracy:[^fn-wilson-score-inversion]

$$\tilde p=\frac{X+z^2/2}{N+z^2},\qquad
[L,U]=\tilde p\pm\frac{z}{N+z^2}\sqrt{\frac{X(N-X)}{N}+\frac{z^2}{4}}.$$ {#eq-wilson-interval}

Here $z$ is the standard normal quantile for the selected two-sided confidence level. Wilson is a frequentist score interval whose nominal coverage describes repeated sampling.

[^fn-wilson-score-inversion]: **Wilson score inversion**\index{Wilson score interval!test inversion}: With $z=z_{1-\alpha/2}$, the score interval contains the values $p\in[0,1]$ satisfying $N(\hat p-p)^2\le z^2p(1-p)$. Solving this quadratic inequality gives the endpoints: the variance uses the hypothesized $p$, rather than fixing it at $\hat p$ as in the Wald construction ([NIST's score-interval derivation](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section2/prc241.htm)).

For zero acceptances in a hypothetical sample of 50 independent tasks, @eq-wilson-interval gives a lower limit of zero and the upper is $z^2/(50+z^2)$, the limit that panel B of @fig-vol3-sample-size-confidence-intervals marks. Read with the outcomes reversed, the same arithmetic prices a clean record: zero observed violations in 50 independent tasks remains consistent with a violation rate up to that upper limit.

Pending, unknown, or unavailable verdicts stay visible, since dropping them biases the sample toward tasks that finish or grade easily. The binary examples here assume complete verdicts; a study with unresolved verdicts declares its cutoff and missing-outcome analysis before counting.

### Compare paired outcomes {#sec-vol3-evaluation-paired}

Run the baseline and candidate configurations on separate, comparably initialized executions of each sampled task, with matched criteria and allowances, and preserve each task's pair of outcomes. @Tbl-vol3-mcnemar-contingency organizes a hypothetical complete comparison whose prespecified cohort is separate from the pending `ws_r19` record; that record was never part of these counts, so leaving it out selects nothing.

| Baseline outcome | Candidate accepted | Candidate rejected |
|:-----------------|:-------------------|:-------------------|
| Accepted         | $n_{11}=70$        | $b=12$             |
| Rejected         | $c=18$             | $n_{00}=50$        |

: **Paired task outcomes**: One baseline run and one candidate run on each of 150 independently sampled tasks. Counts are illustrative, with no missing verdicts; execution order and fixtures follow the prespecified comparison protocol. {#tbl-vol3-mcnemar-contingency}

The baseline's accepted count is $n_{11}+b$ and the candidate's is $n_{11}+c$. The observed difference is

$$\hat\Delta=\hat p_{\mathrm{cand}}-\hat p_{\mathrm{base}}=\frac{c-b}{N}.$$

The discordant pairs determine the net gain. Concordant pairs still contribute to $N$, the acceptance rates, and uncertainty about the population difference. The marginal counts alone do not reveal whether the candidate gained tasks without losing any or exchanged many wins and losses.

**McNemar's test**\index{McNemar's test!definition} addresses equality of the paired marginal probabilities. Conditional on $n_{\mathrm{disc}}=b+c>0$ discordant pairs under the null, candidate wins have a $\operatorname{Binomial}(n_{\mathrm{disc}},1/2)$ distribution. The exact two-sided test used here sums the symmetric tails:

$$p_{\mathrm{exact}}=\min\!\left(1,\;2\sum_{j=0}^{\min(b,c)}\binom{n_{\mathrm{disc}}}{j}2^{-n_{\mathrm{disc}}}\right).$$

The exact form avoids a small-discordance chi-squared approximation. McNemar's test answers an equality question, and a release decision usually asks a magnitude question instead: how much loss is tolerable.

That magnitude question is **noninferiority**\index{Noninferiority!definition}, the claim that the candidate loses no more than a declared tolerance $\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$, and it needs an interval for $\Delta$ itself. The worksheet uses [Newcombe's paired-score method 10](https://www.site.uottawa.ca/~nat/Courses/csi5388/Newcombe.1998.pdf), which combines the two marginal Wilson intervals with a continuity-corrected estimate of their within-pair correlation. The result is an interval for candidate minus baseline, a nominal, approximate interval under independent paired sampling that is valid for one prespecified look.

Let $[L_c,U_c]$ and $[L_b,U_b]$ be the candidate and baseline Wilson intervals. Write $w=n_{11}n_{00}-bc$. The corrected correlation is

$$\phi_* = \frac{w_*}{\sqrt{(n_{11}+c)(b+n_{00})(n_{11}+b)(c+n_{00})}},\qquad
w_* = \begin{cases}\max(w-N/2,0),&w>0,\\w,&w\le0.\end{cases}$$

Set $\phi_*=0$ when the denominator is zero. The paired interval is

$$L_\Delta=\hat\Delta-\sqrt{(\hat p_c-L_c)^2+(U_b-\hat p_b)^2-2\phi_*(\hat p_c-L_c)(U_b-\hat p_b)},$$
$$U_\Delta=\hat\Delta+\sqrt{(U_c-\hat p_c)^2+(\hat p_b-L_b)^2-2\phi_*(U_c-\hat p_c)(\hat p_b-L_b)}.$$

Pairing enters through $\phi_*$: shared task outcomes affect the uncertainty of the difference, even when the two marginal acceptance counts stay fixed.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-paired-comparison
#| echo: false
# PAIRED ACCEPTANCE DIFFERENCE (LEGO)
# Goal: Estimate one rate and compare paired configurations at a fixed endpoint.
# Scope: Illustrative independent task pairs, complete verdicts, fixed protocol.
from math import sqrt, comb, ceil
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, check

def evaluation_wilson(x, n, z):
    if not isinstance(x, int) or not isinstance(n, int) or not 0 <= x <= n or n <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Require integer counts 0 <= x <= n and n > 0")
    center = (x + z * z / 2) / (n + z * z)
    spread = z * sqrt(x * (n - x) / n + z * z / 4) / (n + z * z)
    return max(0.0, center - spread), min(1.0, center + spread)

def evaluation_paired_score(n11, b, c, n00, z):
    # Newcombe (1998), method 10. b=baseline-only; c=candidate-only.
    cells = (n11, b, c, n00)
    if any(not isinstance(v, int) or v < 0 for v in cells) or sum(cells) <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Require nonnegative integer cells and positive total")
    n = sum(cells)
    pc, pb = (n11 + c) / n, (n11 + b) / n
    lc, uc = evaluation_wilson(n11 + c, n, z)
    lb, ub = evaluation_wilson(n11 + b, n, z)
    denominator = sqrt((n11 + c) * (b + n00) * (n11 + b) * (c + n00))
    numerator = n11 * n00 - b * c
    if numerator > 0:
        numerator = max(numerator - n / 2, 0)
    rho = numerator / denominator if denominator else 0.0
    lower_width = sqrt(max(0.0, (pc - lc) ** 2 + (ub - pb) ** 2 - 2 * rho * (pc - lc) * (ub - pb)))
    upper_width = sqrt(max(0.0, (uc - pc) ** 2 + (pb - lb) ** 2 - 2 * rho * (uc - pc) * (pb - lb)))
    return pc - pb, pc - pb - lower_width, pc - pb + upper_width

class PairedAcceptance:
    # 1. LOAD: prespecified illustrative counts, nominal level, and tolerance.
    n11, b, c, n00 = 70, 12, 18, 50
    z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
    tolerance = 0.02  # acceptable loss chosen before seeing outcomes

    # 2. EXECUTE: two-sided interval and exact conditional equality test.
    n = n11 + b + c + n00
    delta, lower, upper = evaluation_paired_score(n11, b, c, n00, z)
    discordant = b + c
    tail_count = 0
    for j in range(min(b, c) + 1):
        tail_count += comb(discordant, j)
    exact_p = min(1.0, 2 * tail_count / 2**discordant) if discordant else 1.0
    noninferiority = lower > -tolerance
    zero_upper = evaluation_wilson(0, 50, z)[1]
    # Planning: lower half-width scales as 1/sqrt(N); what N clears the margin?
    lower_width = delta - lower
    n_if_gain_holds = ceil(n * (lower_width / (delta + tolerance)) ** 2)
    n_if_no_gain = ceil(n * (lower_width / tolerance) ** 2)

    # 3. GUARD: arithmetic plus independent published method-10 examples.
    check(n == 150 and n11 + b == 82 and n11 + c == 88, "Paired totals")
    check(abs(delta - 0.04) < 1e-12, "Candidate-minus-baseline direction")
    check(abs(lower - (-0.032062854)) < 1e-8 and abs(upper - 0.111211210) < 1e-8, "Worksheet interval")
    check(not noninferiority and lower < 0 < upper, "Inconclusive gate and superiority")
    check(abs(zero_upper - z * z / (50 + z * z)) < 1e-12, "Wilson zero-count algebra")
    check(n < n_if_gain_holds < 2 * n < n_if_no_gain, "Planning counts ordered")
    for cells, expected in [((20, 2, 12, 16), (0.0562, 0.3292)), ((27, 0, 0, 27), (-0.0351, 0.0351))]:
        _, lo, hi = evaluation_paired_score(*cells, z)
        check(abs(lo - expected[0]) < 0.00005 and abs(hi - expected[1]) < 0.00005, "Newcombe Table III")

    # 4. OUTPUT: all formatted exports are consumed below.
    n_str = fmt_int(n)
    b_str, c_str = fmt_int(b), fmt_int(c)
    zero_upper_str = fmt_percent(zero_upper, precision=2, style="prose")
    delta_pp_str = fmt_int(round(100 * delta))
    lower_pp_str = fmt(100 * lower, precision=2)
    upper_pp_str = fmt(100 * upper, precision=2)
    tolerance_pp_str = fmt(100 * tolerance, precision=0)
    exact_p_str = fmt(exact_p, precision=3)
    lower_width_pp_str = fmt(100 * lower_width, precision=2)
    clear_width_pp_str = fmt(100 * (delta + tolerance), precision=0)
    n_if_gain_holds_str = fmt_int(n_if_gain_holds)
    n_if_no_gain_str = fmt_int(round(n_if_no_gain, -2))
```

::: {#nbk-vol3-evaluation-wilson-superiority .callout-notebook title="A paired gain and an inconclusive gate"}

**Problem**: For the `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_str` task pairs in @tbl-vol3-mcnemar-contingency, does the candidate establish noninferiority under a prespecified tolerance of `{python} PairedAcceptance.tolerance_pp_str` percentage points, that is, $L_\Delta>-\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$ for the lower endpoint of a nominal 95 percent paired-score interval? If not, how many pairs would the gate need?

**Math**: The observed gain is $\hat\Delta=(c-b)/N=$ (`{python} PairedAcceptance.c_str` $-$ `{python} PairedAcceptance.b_str`)/`{python} PairedAcceptance.n_str`, or `{python} PairedAcceptance.delta_pp_str` points. Method 10 gives the interval from `{python} PairedAcceptance.lower_pp_str` to `{python} PairedAcceptance.upper_pp_str` points, so the lower half-width $\hat\Delta-L_\Delta$ is `{python} PairedAcceptance.lower_width_pp_str` points. Clearing the gate needs that half-width below $\hat\Delta+\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$, `{python} PairedAcceptance.clear_width_pp_str` points. Half-widths shrink as $1/\sqrt N$, so the required count is $N'\approx N\left[(\hat\Delta-L_\Delta)/(\hat\Delta+\delta_{\mathrm{tol}})\right]^2$.

**Result**: The lower endpoint lies below $-\delta_{\mathrm{tol}}$, so the gate is not met, and the interval includes zero, so superiority is not established either. If the observed gain and discordance held, $N'$ comes to about `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_if_gain_holds_str` pairs. The exact two-sided McNemar value, `{python} PairedAcceptance.exact_p_str`, answers the separate equality question.

**Systems insight**: The candidate is held, and the knob that moves the decision is the planned number of pairs, which scales with the square of the lower half-width over the margin still to be cleared. A `{python} PairedAcceptance.delta_pp_str`-point gain that holds needs `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_if_gain_holds_str` pairs; a true gain of zero needs the half-width inside the `{python} PairedAcceptance.tolerance_pp_str`-point tolerance itself, about `{python} PairedAcceptance.n_if_no_gain_str` pairs. Plan that count before collecting data, because rerunning the same comparison until one look passes is a different, uncalibrated test.

:::

The width of an interval is the scale on which every evaluation claim is made. For one rate, the normal approximation gives a half-width of about $z\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}$, largest at $p=1/2$. Precision therefore improves only as $1/\sqrt{N}$, so halving the half-width requires four times as many tasks. Detecting a difference is more demanding than estimating a rate. For two independent arms with average acceptance probability $\bar p$, target difference $\Delta$, two-sided significance $\alpha$, and power $1-\beta$, a standard planning estimate of the tasks needed per arm is

$$N_{\text{arm}}\approx\frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2\,\bar p(1-\bar p)}{\Delta^2}.$$ {#eq-vol3-eval-planning-power}

@Sec-vol3-appendix-math-bootstrap derives the pooled form of @eq-vol3-eval-planning-power and states its assumptions.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-sample-size-scale
#| echo: false
# HOW MANY TASKS A CLAIM NEEDS (LEGO)
# Goal: Give the magnitude of one-rate precision, two-arm detection, and pairing.
# Scope: Planning approximations at hypothetical rates; independent tasks.
from math import sqrt, ceil
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.physics.statistics import calc_two_proportion_sample_size
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

class SampleSizeScale:
    # 1. LOAD: worst-case rate, targets, and the worked paired table's cells.
    p_half = 0.5
    z95 = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
    small_n = 100
    target_half_width = 0.02
    alpha, power = 0.05, 0.80
    z_alpha, z_beta = 1.96, 0.84  # rounded quantiles for these targets
    delta_large, delta_small = 0.04, 0.02
    n11, b, c, n00 = 70, 12, 18, 50  # the worked paired-outcome table

    # 2. EXECUTE: one-rate half-widths, two-arm counts, paired variance.
    half_small = z95 * sqrt(p_half * (1 - p_half) / small_n)
    wilson_lo, wilson_hi = evaluation_wilson(50, small_n, z95)
    wilson_half_small = (wilson_hi - wilson_lo) / 2
    n_for_target = ceil(z95**2 * p_half * (1 - p_half) / target_half_width**2)
    arm_large = calc_two_proportion_sample_size(p_half, delta_large, z_alpha=z_alpha, z_beta=z_beta)
    arm_small = calc_two_proportion_sample_size(p_half, delta_small, z_alpha=z_alpha, z_beta=z_beta)
    arm_large_n, arm_small_n = round(arm_large), round(arm_small)
    pairs = n11 + b + c + n00
    p_cand, p_base = (n11 + c) / pairs, (n11 + b) / pairs
    discordant = (b + c) / pairs
    diff = p_cand - p_base
    var_paired = discordant - diff**2
    var_independent = p_cand * (1 - p_cand) + p_base * (1 - p_base)
    paired_share = var_paired / var_independent
    paired_half = z95 * sqrt(var_paired / pairs)
    independent_mult = var_independent / var_paired

    # 3. GUARD: scaling law, published-formula arithmetic, and pairing algebra.
    check(abs(NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2) - z_alpha) < 0.005, "Rounded significance quantile")
    check(abs(NormalDist().inv_cdf(power) - z_beta) < 0.005, "Rounded power quantile")
    check(abs(half_small - 0.098) < 0.0005, "Half-width at N=100, p=0.5")
    check(abs(wilson_half_small - half_small) < 0.003, "Wilson close to normal at p=0.5")
    check(n_for_target == 2401, "Tasks for a 2-point half-width")
    check(abs(arm_large - 2450) < 1e-6 and abs(arm_small - 9800) < 1e-6, "Two-arm planning counts")
    check(abs(arm_small / arm_large - 4) < 1e-9, "Halving the difference quadruples N")
    check(abs(discordant - 0.2) < 1e-12 and abs(diff - 0.04) < 1e-12, "Worked-table discordance")
    check(0.35 < paired_share < 0.45, "Pairing removes most of the variance")
    check(abs(paired_half - 0.0713) < 0.0005, "Matches the worked interval's scale")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    small_n_str = fmt_int(small_n)
    alpha_str = fmt_percent(alpha, precision=0, style="prose")
    power_str = fmt_percent(power, precision=0, style="prose")
    half_small_pp_str = fmt(100 * half_small, precision=1)
    wilson_half_pp_str = fmt(100 * wilson_half_small, precision=1)
    target_pp_str = fmt(100 * target_half_width, precision=0)
    n_for_target_str = fmt_int(n_for_target)
    delta_large_pp_str = fmt(100 * delta_large, precision=0)
    delta_small_pp_str = fmt(100 * delta_small, precision=0)
    arm_large_str = fmt_int(arm_large_n)
    arm_small_str = fmt_int(arm_small_n)
    discordant_str = fmt_percent(discordant, precision=0, style="prose")
    paired_share_str = fmt_percent(round(paired_share, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    paired_half_pp_str = fmt(100 * paired_half, precision=1)
    independent_mult_str = fmt_multiple(independent_mult, precision=1)
```

The magnitudes follow directly. At $p=0.5$ and 95 percent confidence, `{python} SampleSizeScale.small_n_str` independent tasks give a half-width of about `{python} SampleSizeScale.half_small_pp_str` percentage points (the Wilson interval gives `{python} SampleSizeScale.wilson_half_pp_str`), and a half-width of `{python} SampleSizeScale.target_pp_str` points needs `{python} SampleSizeScale.n_for_target_str` tasks. With a `{python} SampleSizeScale.alpha_str` two-sided significance target and `{python} SampleSizeScale.power_str` power at $\bar p=0.5$, @eq-vol3-eval-planning-power asks for about `{python} SampleSizeScale.arm_large_str` tasks per arm to detect a `{python} SampleSizeScale.delta_large_pp_str`-point difference and `{python} SampleSizeScale.arm_small_str` per arm for a `{python} SampleSizeScale.delta_small_pp_str`-point difference. The count that estimates one rate to the narrower half-width and the count that detects the larger difference are similar in size, but they answer different questions. @Fig-vol3-sample-size-confidence-intervals plots that $1/\sqrt{N}$ contraction and, at a small sample, shows where the Wald interval fails and the Wilson interval does not.

::: {#fig-vol3-sample-size-confidence-intervals fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**How Many Tasks an Interval Needs**: Panel A plots the normal-approximation half-width at 95 percent confidence against the number of independent tasks for three acceptance probabilities. At $p=0.5$, `{python} SampleSizeScale.small_n_str` tasks give about $\pm$`{python} SampleSizeScale.half_small_pp_str` points, and `{python} SampleSizeScale.n_for_target_str` tasks reach the dashed $\pm$`{python} SampleSizeScale.target_pp_str`-point target. Panel B compares Wald and Wilson intervals, in percent, for 50 tasks. With no acceptances, the Wald interval collapses to zero width, while the Wilson upper limit is `{python} PairedAcceptance.zero_upper_str`. With two acceptances, the Wald lower limit falls below zero, an impossible probability. At 25 acceptances the two intervals nearly coincide." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A: line chart of normal-approximation half-width in points, from 0 to 20, against independent tasks from 0 to 2,500, with a solid curve for p equal to 0.5, a dashed curve for 0.2, and a dotted curve for 0.05. All three fall steeply and then flatten. Two points on the p equal to 0.5 curve are labeled, one at 100 tasks and one where the curve meets a dashed horizontal line at 2 points. Panel B: three rows of horizontal interval bars at 50 tasks, each comparing a gray Wald interval with a blue Wilson interval. With 0 successes, Wald is a single point at zero, labeled zero width, and Wilson extends from zero to a labeled upper limit. With 2 successes, the Wald bar extends into a shaded region below zero, labeled lower limit below 0, and the Wilson bar stays above zero. With 25 successes, the two bars nearly coincide around 50 percent."}
![](images/svg/sample_size_confidence_intervals.svg)
:::

Pairing changes the count. Each task's candidate-minus-baseline outcome takes the value $-1$, $0$, or $+1$, so with discordant fraction $\psi$ the paired estimate has variance $(\psi-\Delta^2)/N$. The worked table has `{python} SampleSizeScale.discordant_str` discordant pairs, which puts the paired variance at about `{python} SampleSizeScale.paired_share_str` of the variance two independent arms would have at the same acceptance rates. The same precision therefore needs well under half as many tasks, and the worked interval spans about $\pm$`{python} SampleSizeScale.paired_half_pp_str` points, as the worked comparison found. The discordance rate is a planning assumption until the study observes it.

Estimation, detection, and noninferiority are different objectives with different counts, and a paired design also depends on expected discordance. Plan with plausible effect and dependence assumptions before the study, then report the observed interval and the actual protocol.

The comparison so far uses one run per configuration per task. Multiple permitted attempts change what success means and what it costs. The next section distinguishes finding at least one acceptable candidate from consistent execution and acceptance under a fixed budget.

### Potential and repeated-run consistency {#sec-vol3-evaluation-pass-k}

The unit of replication also determines what a repeated-run metric means. A pool containing one acceptable repair, a selector returning that repair, and a system completing the same task reliably are three different outcomes. @Sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k defined pass@$k$ as candidate availability, the probability that a pool of $k$ runs contains a passing member. Work that recurs, such as the same policy question answered in session after session, needs the opposite quantifier: every run must pass. The two belong in one statement, because they move in opposite directions as $k$ grows.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k-collapse
#| echo: false
# REPEATED-RUN CONSISTENCY ON ONE TASK (LEGO)
# Goal: Show how quickly all-k consistency falls below single-run success.
# Scope: One fixed task, independent runs under the declared reset.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

class PassPowK:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical single-run acceptance probabilities and recurrences.
    p_hi, p_lo = 0.90, 0.80
    p_better = 0.95  # after halving the single-run failure rate
    k = 8
    target = 0.90  # consistency the recurring work must hold
    chk_p, chk_k = 0.95, 5  # checkpoint exercise givens

    # 2. EXECUTE
    pow_hi, pow_lo, pow_better = p_hi**k, p_lo**k, p_better**k
    at_k_hi = 1 - (1 - p_hi) ** k
    p_needed = target ** (1 / k)
    fail_cut = (1 - p_hi) / (1 - p_needed)

    # 3. GUARD
    check(0.42 < pow_hi < 0.44 and 0.16 < pow_lo < 0.18, "Eight-run consistency")
    check(at_k_hi > 0.999, "Availability near one")
    check(0.986 < p_needed < 0.988 and 7 < fail_cut < 8, "Rate needed for the target")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    p_hi_str = fmt(p_hi, precision=1)
    p_hi_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_hi, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_lo_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_lo, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_better_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_better, precision=0, style="prose")
    k_str = fmt_int(k)
    target_str = fmt_percent(target, precision=0, style="prose")
    pow_hi_str = fmt_percent(round(pow_hi, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    pow_lo_str = fmt_percent(round(pow_lo, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    pow_better_str = fmt_percent(round(pow_better, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    at_k_hi_str = fmt_percent(round(at_k_hi, 4), precision=0, style="prose")
    p_needed_str = fmt_percent(p_needed, precision=1, style="prose")
    fail_needed_str = fmt_percent(1 - p_needed, precision=1, style="prose")
    fail_cut_mult_str = fmt_multiple(fail_cut, precision=1)
    chk_p_str = fmt_percent(chk_p, precision=0, style="prose")
    chk_k_str = fmt_int(chk_k)
```

::: {#thrm-vol3-evaluation-pass-at-k-pass-pow-k .callout-theorem title="Availability and consistency over repeated runs"}

*For a fixed task $i$, initial-state distribution, complete generation policy, and binary pass criterion, let runs be independent and identically distributed given the task, each passing with probability $p_i$.* Averaged over the declared task distribution, the probability that at least one of $k$ runs passes and the probability that all $k$ pass, **pass$^k$** or **repeated-run consistency**\index{Repeated-run consistency!definition}, are estimated from $n_i\ge k$ fully graded runs with $c_i$ passes by the unbiased subset estimators [@chen2021evaluating]

$$\operatorname{pass@}k=\mathbb{E}_i\left[1-(1-p_i)^k\right],\qquad
\widehat q_{i,k}=1-\frac{\binom{n_i-c_i}{k}}{\binom{n_i}{k}},$$ {#eq-pass-at-k}

$$\operatorname{pass}^{k}=\mathbb{E}_i\left[p_i^k\right],\qquad
\widehat r_{i,k}=\frac{\binom{c_i}{k}}{\binom{n_i}{k}}.$$ {#eq-pass-pow-k}

*   **Task pass probability** ($p_i$): Single-run acceptance under the declared reset and grading protocol.
*   **Claim size** ($k$): Runs the claim covers, a pool for pass@$k$ and recurrences for pass$^k$.
*   **Graded runs** ($n_i$, $c_i$): Runs generated for the estimate and the number that passed; each binomial numerator is zero when $n_i-c_i<k$ or $c_i<k$, respectively.

**Pitfall**: *pass@$k$ rises with $k$ while pass$^k$ falls.* The same system can look near perfect or unreliable depending on which quantifier the claim needs, as notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k} shows numerically.

:::

Each subset in @eq-pass-at-k contributes one when it contains a pass, and each in @eq-pass-pow-k when all its members pass, so their expectations are $1-(1-p_i)^k$ and $p_i^k$; @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pass-at-k derives both by indicator averaging and gives product forms that avoid factorial overflow. Average task-level estimates with the declared task weights, never by repeat count. Generating exactly $n_i=k$ is valid and makes the estimate the indicator of this one pool. The pass@$k$ metric measures candidate availability, while the deployed selector's returned results and abstentions are measured separately, as @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k established. The pass$^k$ metric can describe complete system runs, selector included, when that complete policy is what each run executes. The consistency metric pass$^k$ entered agent benchmarking with $\tau$-bench, which reports it for tool-using agents in customer-service domains [@yao2024taubench].

::: {#nbk-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k .callout-notebook title="Single-run success is not reliability"}

**Problem**: A system accepts a recurring task on `{python} PassPowK.p_hi_pct_str` of single runs. How often does it pass all `{python} PassPowK.k_str` recurrences, and what single-run rate would hold `{python} PassPowK.target_str` consistency?

**Math**: By @eq-pass-pow-k for one task, pass$^k=p^k$. With $p$ equal to `{python} PassPowK.p_hi_str` and $k$ equal to `{python} PassPowK.k_str`, that is about `{python} PassPowK.pow_hi_str`; at `{python} PassPowK.p_lo_pct_str` it falls to about `{python} PassPowK.pow_lo_str`. Availability over the same runs, $1-(1-p)^k$, is effectively `{python} PassPowK.at_k_hi_str`. Holding `{python} PassPowK.target_str` requires $p\ge P_{\text{target}}^{1/k}$, about `{python} PassPowK.p_needed_str`.

**Systems insight**: Recurrences compound exactly as turns do in @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, so consistency is set by the single-run failure rate raised to the number of recurrences. Halving that failure rate to reach `{python} PassPowK.p_better_pct_str` lifts pass$^k$ only to `{python} PassPowK.pow_better_str`; holding `{python} PassPowK.target_str` needs single-run failure of `{python} PassPowK.fail_needed_str`, a `{python} PassPowK.fail_cut_mult_str` cut. Recurring work therefore buys reliability most cheaply with a check that catches a failed run before delivery, which turns a failed recurrence into a retry.

:::

The distance between the two quantifiers, availability near one against consistency of `{python} PassPowK.pow_hi_str`, is the **verification gap**\index{Verification gap!definition}. A selector with a reliable checker converts availability into one accepted delivery at the cost priced in @sec-vol3-evaluation-matched-budgets; work that must pass every time it recurs gets only consistency.

A sequence of $k$ independently drawn *new tasks* has all-success probability $(\mathbb{E}_i[p_i])^k$, which Jensen's inequality places at or below $\mathbb{E}_i[p_i^k]$, so repeating one task overstates consistency across new tasks whenever difficulty varies. Shared outages, state carried between runs, or feedback-conditioned revisions break these independence formulas. The sampling units in @tbl-vol3-statistical-metrics distinguish a complete policy trial from repeated independent runs; relabeling an adaptive repair policy's turns as runs leaves its experiment unchanged.

| Reported quantity   | Sampling unit and question                                                               | What it does not establish                          |
|:--------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| pass@$k$            | One task's pool: does at least one member pass the declared criterion?                   | That the deployed selector returns it within budget |
| Selected acceptance | One complete system trial: does the actual returned result meet the acceptance contract? | That every future run or task will pass             |
| pass$^k$            | One task repeated $k$ times: do all runs pass?                                           | Success across $k$ independently drawn new tasks    |
| Budgeted acceptance | One complete policy trial under stated resource limits                                   | The best score achievable by any policy             |

: **Metrics name different experiments**: The criterion, task distribution, reset and dependence assumptions, and treatment of unresolved verdicts accompany every score. {#tbl-vol3-statistical-metrics}

The subset formulas require binary labels for the declared pool, so a pending or unavailable verdict stays in $n_i$ under the prespecified cutoff and missing-outcome policy. Where acceptance remains unknown, report that count and the bounds obtained by assigning unresolved cases to either outcome.

Which row of @tbl-vol3-statistical-metrics a claim needs depends on how the work is used, and the four lighthouse workloads (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}, \ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}, \ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}, and \ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) use it differently.

::: {#lhs-vol3-evaluation-evidence-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Evidence standard by archetype"}

| Workload          | Checker the task admits                                              | Metric the claim needs                                                       | Binding evidence limit                                                   |
|:------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Repair agent      | Sealed regression and defect tests on the exact submitted artifact   | Selected acceptance under budget; pass@$k$ only with the checker in the loop | Test coverage, and grader isolation from submitted code                  |
| Research agent    | Rubric scored by a calibrated judge; citation checks against sources | Selected acceptance with the judge's error rates reported                    | Judge false-acceptance rate on untrusted retrieved content               |
| Remediation agent | State-delta checks on an isolated replica; approval records          | pass$^k$ over recurring incident classes, with zero forbidden effects        | Irreversible writes that no shadow fixture can exercise                  |
| Support agent     | Policy-grounded rubric per answer                                    | pass$^k$ across sessions asking the same policy question                     | Consistency over many short sessions, measured only on live-like traffic |

: **Evidence standard by workload**: Each workload's checker determines which metric its claims can support, and each carries a different limit on what its evaluation can establish. {#tbl-vol3-evaluation-evidence-by-archetype}

**Systems insight**: @Tbl-vol3-evaluation-evidence-by-archetype shows that the archetype decides the quantifier. The repair agent can buy acceptance with checked retries, so its evaluation reports selected acceptance and prices it through $C_{\text{eff}}$. The support agent cannot retry a wrong policy answer once a customer has read it, so its claim is pass$^k$, which notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-evaluation-pass-pow-k} showed falling far below single-run accuracy. The research agent's number is only as good as its judge's calibration, and the remediation agent's release rests on hard limits that statistics cannot supply.

:::

### Comparing at matched budgets {#sec-vol3-evaluation-matched-budgets}

Fix the task distribution, criteria, and comparison envelope before comparing policies. If the experiment isolates a prompt change, hold the other relevant configuration and allowances fixed. If it compares complete policies, each may allocate the same resource envelope differently among generation, checking, and repair. Equal budgets need not mean equal realized sample counts. Report both allowances and actual use, including time and tokens separately from monetary charges.

For a fixed complete policy $\pi$, let $\mathrm{Acc}_\pi$ indicate accepted completion under the declared criteria, $C_\pi$ its total monetary charge, and $B$ a monetary ceiling. Its budgeted acceptance is

$$q_\pi(B)=\Pr(\mathrm{Acc}_\pi=1\ \land\ C_\pi\le B).$$

Token and elapsed-time ceilings add separate conditions in their own units. The quantity evaluates $\pi$ as specified, and its accounting covers generation, grading, failed attempts, started work that is later discarded, and required cleanup within the declared measurement boundary. Unknown charges count as outstanding liabilities. The admission and finalization guards of @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting keep enforcing their bounds whatever the measured average.

Observed cost per accepted task is the total charge for all initiated trials divided by their accepted count. Its population counterpart is $C_{\text{eff}}$ from @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task, with $\mathbb{E}[C_\pi]$ as the attempt cost and $\Pr(\mathrm{Acc}_\pi=1)$ as $p_{\text{acc}}$. The ratio charges failed trials to accepted ones, so it never falls below the mean cost of the successful trials alone. A cohort with no accepted tasks reports its spend and the zero count, and unsettled costs carry an explicit provisional boundary.

Consider a restricted comparison with independent, isolated candidates, constant pass probability $p>0$, generation cost $g$, checking cost $v$, and a checker that decides the stipulated criterion exactly. All costs are in dollars. A selector that returns the first passing candidate reaches availability $q_k=1-(1-p)^k$. Generating and checking all $k$ candidates costs $k(g+v)$.
