Generating and checking sequentially, stopping at the first pass or after $k$ failures, starts an expected

$$\mathbb{E}[N_k]=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-p)^j=\frac{q_k}{p}$$

candidates. The all-fail path still starts exactly $k$, so the policy is bounded. Consequently,

$$C_{\text{eff,batch}}=\frac{k(g+v)}{q_k},\qquad
C_{\text{eff,seq}}=\frac{g+v}{p}.$$ {#eq-cost-per-accepted-task-iid}

Generating all candidates first and only stopping *checking* early is a third policy: its expected cost is $kg+(q_k/p)v$. Generation already performed stays paid for. The formulas in @eq-cost-per-accepted-task-iid omit latency constraints, checker errors, task heterogeneity, and adaptive feedback, and at $p=0$ both policies exhaust their cap with no finite ratio.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-metrics-and-selection
#| echo: false
# METRIC UNITS AND BOUNDED SELECTION COST (LEGO)
# Goal: Separate same-task consistency from new-task sequences, then price selection.
# Scope: Hypothetical probabilities, exact stipulated checker, equal fixed unit costs.
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_usd, check

class SelectionMetrics:
    # 1. LOAD: two equally weighted task types; separate fixed-task cost scenario.
    task_probabilities = (0.5, 0.9)
    repetitions = 2
    p = 0.4
    k = 3
    generation = 0.03 * USD
    verification = 0.01 * USD

    # 2. EXECUTE: population thought experiment, not observed benchmark data.
    mean_p = sum(task_probabilities) / len(task_probabilities)
    same_all = 0.0
    for task_p in task_probabilities:
        same_all += task_p**repetitions / len(task_probabilities)
    new_all = mean_p**repetitions
    q = 1 - (1 - p) ** k
    expected_n = q / p
    unit = generation + verification
    batch = k * unit
    sequential = expected_n * unit
    batch_per_accepted = batch / q
    sequential_per_accepted = sequential / q
    doubled_p_per_accepted = unit / (2 * p)  # sequential policy, generator twice as good

    # 3. GUARD: endpoints, path cap, and independent arithmetic identities.
    check(0 < p < 1 and k >= 1, "Finite positive acceptance probability")
    check(abs(same_all - 0.53) < 1e-12 and abs(new_all - 0.49) < 1e-12, "Different sampling units")
    check(abs(q - 0.784) < 1e-12 and abs(expected_n - 1.96) < 1e-12, "Capped search")
    check(1 <= expected_n <= k and sequential <= batch, "Bounded expected work")
    check(abs(sequential_per_accepted.to(USD).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-12, "Cost includes failed trials")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed below.
    task_probs_str = " and ".join(fmt_percent(x, precision=0, style="prose") for x in task_probabilities)
    repetitions_str = fmt_int(repetitions)
    same_all_str = fmt_percent(same_all, precision=0, style="prose")
    new_all_str = fmt_percent(new_all, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, precision=0, style="prose")
    k_str = fmt_int(k)
    generation_str = fmt_usd(generation, precision=2)
    verification_str = fmt_usd(verification, precision=2)
    q_str = fmt_percent(q, precision=1, style="prose")
    expected_n_str = fmt(expected_n, precision=2)
    batch_str = fmt_usd(batch, precision=2)
    sequential_str = fmt_usd(sequential, precision=4)
    batch_accepted_str = fmt_usd(batch_per_accepted, precision=3)
    sequential_accepted_str = fmt_usd(sequential_per_accepted, precision=2)
    doubled_p_accepted_str = fmt_usd(doubled_p_per_accepted, precision=2)
    batch_premium_str = fmt_percent(round(float((batch_per_accepted / sequential_per_accepted).to("").magnitude) - 1, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-13-metrics-and-selection .callout-notebook title="Which experiment, and which cost?"}

**Problem**: How does changing the sampling unit change all-run consistency, and how does stopping generation early change cost at the same candidate cap?

**Metric assumptions and result**: Suppose two equally likely task types have pass probabilities `{python} SelectionMetrics.task_probs_str`. Runs are independent conditional on type. Repeating one randomly selected task `{python} SelectionMetrics.repetitions_str` times gives all-run consistency `{python} SelectionMetrics.same_all_str`. Drawing a new independent task for every run gives `{python} SelectionMetrics.new_all_str`. The single-run average is the same; the experiment is not.

**Cost assumptions**: Separately, use a fixed-task pass probability of `{python} SelectionMetrics.p_str`, at most `{python} SelectionMetrics.k_str` isolated candidates, generation cost `{python} SelectionMetrics.generation_str`, and exact checking cost `{python} SelectionMetrics.verification_str` per candidate. Costs cover each started candidate's generation and check and nothing else, both policies have time to finish their capped work, and acceptance means this stipulated check.

**Math**: Both policies return a passing candidate with probability `{python} SelectionMetrics.q_str`. Full batch generation and checking cost `{python} SelectionMetrics.batch_str` per initiated trial. Sequential generation and checking start `{python} SelectionMetrics.expected_n_str` candidates on average and cost `{python} SelectionMetrics.sequential_str`. Either policy's all-fail path incurs the full batch cost. Charging failed trials to accepted ones gives approximately `{python} SelectionMetrics.batch_accepted_str` for the batch policy versus `{python} SelectionMetrics.sequential_accepted_str` for sequential early stopping.

**Systems insight**: Under sequential stopping, $C_{\text{eff}}=(g+v)/p$ whatever the cap, so raising the cap buys acceptance probability at no increase in cost per accepted task, while the full batch here pays a `{python} SelectionMetrics.batch_premium_str` premium for the same acceptance. The one knob that lowers $C_{\text{eff}}$ is the single-candidate pass probability: doubling $p$ halves it, to `{python} SelectionMetrics.doubled_p_accepted_str`. An imperfect selector, a deadline, or a shared environment changes these formulas and is measured as part of the policy.

:::

Choosing a generator therefore reduces to comparing $(g+v)/p$ from @eq-cost-per-accepted-task-iid across generators, rather than choosing $k$. When checking is cheap, a cheaper generator with a lower $p$ wins if its generation saving outweighs the extra attempts; when checking dominates, raising $p$ upstream wins because every failed attempt pays for a check. @Sec-vol3-test-time-compute-computation-allocation treats how to allocate that generation compute across tasks of different difficulty.

::: {#chk-vol3-evaluation-statistics .callout-checkpoint title="Statistical evidence"}

- [ ] **Unit of replication**: Your suite already runs each task more times than $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{run}}/\sigma^2_{\mathrm{task}}$. Should the next evaluation budget buy repeats or new tasks, and why?
- [ ] **Comparison evidence**: How do estimation precision, planned detection power, and an observed paired difference answer different questions?
- [ ] **Potential and selection**: A pool contains a passing patch but the selector returns another. Which metric records the available pass, and which records the delivered failure?
- [ ] **Consistency estimate**: A support agent answers a refund-policy question correctly on `{python} PassPowK.chk_p_str` of single runs. Estimate pass$^k$ over `{python} PassPowK.chk_k_str` sessions, and the single-run rate that would hold `{python} PassPowK.target_str` consistency over those sessions.
- [ ] **Budget accounting**: Why must generating all candidates before checking be priced differently from generating only after the preceding candidate fails?

:::

These metrics quantify outcomes under a declared experiment, and explaining an individual failure takes different evidence. A lower acceptance rate could arise from the model, missing context, an observation boundary, or a slow dependency. Tracing supplies the execution evidence needed to investigate those possibilities.

## Distributed Trajectory Tracing {#sec-vol3-evaluation-tracing}

A comparison can show that a candidate system completes fewer tasks or takes longer under the declared evaluation conditions and still leave open which interaction deserves investigation. For the connection-pool repair, a long test wait, a delayed model response, and a gap before the final report can all contribute to elapsed time. A trace connects those observations to the particular trial, candidate, and operations rather than leaving them as unrelated service logs.

**Distributed tracing**\index{Distributed tracing!definition} records related units of work across component boundaries. Dapper established the trace-and-span model at production scale [@sigelman2010dapper]. A **span**\index{Span!definition} describes one observed operation with an identity, start and end boundaries, attributes, and optional timed events. Parent relationships express nesting; links can connect asynchronous work that does not fit one nested lifetime. These are the basic abstractions provided by [OpenTelemetry traces](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/). A model call, a mediated tool attempt, and a later result-processing step can be separate spans within one trajectory.

The resulting record is evidence about observed execution, and missing instrumentation or dropped records can hide an operation that occurred.

### Separate diagnostic capture from recovery history

::: {#psp-13-telemetry-duality .callout-perspective title="Recovery history and diagnostic traces"}

The trajectory log in @sec-vol3-durable-execution preserves the acknowledged history and artifacts required to reconstruct selected state under a declared failure domain. A compatible checkpoint, complete required suffix, and available referenced bytes support that promise. A monitoring copy that shares their identifiers is no substitute.

Diagnostic traces instead support timing analysis, comparison, and investigation. Their capture and retention policies can omit records or payloads. The same observation can contribute to both systems, but its obligations differ: sampling may discard an optional span while the authoritative operation identity, uncertainty, and reservation remain required for recovery.

:::

The surviving intent for `test_r18`, attempt `attempt1`, stays unresolved until adequate result evidence arrives, and a diagnostic span ending at a timeout settles nothing. A later authenticated result updates its ledger without restarting a held continuation. The trace should correlate that evidence with the original attempt and the later processing step, preserving both lifetimes.

Captured content has a similar boundary. The delivered-input manifest records what a particular model invocation actually received. An optional raw output may contain more than that bounded observation; a newly assembled prompt may contain something different. Use the recorded delivered version when investigating the historical call. As @sec-vol3-persistence-replay established, a hash verifies available bytes but cannot reconstruct missing content. Exact replay requires its declared inputs to remain available under authorized access, not merely an index of their hashes.

### Record the identities and decisions that answer a question

A small consistent schema is more useful than a long list of fields whose meanings differ between producers. @Tbl-vol3-trace-evidence-fields groups the information needed to connect a trial's measurements to its evidence. The groups are conceptual rather than a required vocabulary, and immutable references can join shared records when their availability and access policy support the intended analysis.

| Record group          | Information to preserve                                                                                                                    | Question it answers                                                                 |
|:----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Evaluation identity   | Task identity, trial identity, fixture and criterion versions, system configuration, candidate artifact revision                           | Which experiment and candidate does this observation concern?                       |
| Observed work         | Trace and span identities, operation kind, producer, start/end boundary, clock domain, parent or dependency links                          | Which work was observed, where, and in relation to what other work?                 |
| Admission and attempt | Model invocation or logical operation identity, transport attempt, applicable decision and policy references                               | Was this proposal withheld or admitted, and which attempt produced the evidence?    |
| Outcome and usage     | Response status and source, evidence scope, observed token/tool usage, unresolved liability, task-verdict reference                        | What is known about the operation, its costs, and the separate acceptance decision? |
| Capture limits        | Delivered-input and observation references, omitted ranges or bytes, instrumentation version, known drops, retention/access classification | What can an investigator inspect, and what does this record leave unavailable?      |

: **Minimal trace evidence groups**: Keep identities, observed facts, runtime decisions, and capture limits distinguishable. A completed span is not a completed task. {#tbl-vol3-trace-evidence-fields}

The schema carries the task, trial, configuration, and artifact distinctions established by the acceptance record into each observed interaction. Provider provenance should state what the interface exposes, rather than infer a physical model checkpoint from a mutable service name.

A successful process exit can accompany a partial observation, and a complete response can report a failed check. Keep those fields separate from the task's pass, fail, pending, or unknown verdict. An acceptance decision may arrive after the execution span closes. Its criterion version and evidence references belong to that later decision; a generic span status cannot substitute for them. Actual charges and unresolved reservations likewise remain distinct.

Across a gateway, queue, or sandbox boundary, record the relationship between dispatched work and the corresponding response or callback. A standard carrier such as [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) can convey correlation information between participating components. Trace identifiers correlate records and carry no authority, so admission, authentication, and result checks stay with the runtime, and an incoming carrier's asserted identity is never authoritative. Restrict propagation to appropriate recipients and keep sensitive task data out of correlation headers. If a tool cannot emit trustworthy internal spans, a host-observed dispatch-to-response interval remains useful; label that boundary instead of inventing internal stages.

### Read overlap and missing time before attributing latency

A parent span can enclose its children. Adding the parent's duration to every child therefore double-counts time. Concurrent children also overlap. Ordering comes from a completion dependency, never from a parent link alone. For asynchronous work, record the dispatch, response, and join conditions that determine when dependent work can proceed.

Durations measured on one monotonic clock can be compared within that clock domain. Timestamps from different hosts require a stated synchronization or alignment model; apparent overlap or reversed order can otherwise reflect clock error. Instrumentation boundaries matter even without skew. Client-observed model latency can include transport, queueing, and generation. Time to first token is not an isolated measurement of prefill, and a host-observed tool wait is not necessarily executor CPU time.

A critical-path calculation uses the dependency graph and elapsed intervals at a declared boundary. Sequential required stages add; branches that start together and must all finish contribute their longest duration. Delayed starts, resource contention, or unobserved dependencies require a different calculation. The following notebook makes those assumptions explicit.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-observed-critical-path
#| echo: false
# OBSERVED SPANS AND A CHANGING CRITICAL PATH (LEGO)
# Goal: Separate overlapping work, unexplained time, and a conditional speedup.
# Scope: Hypothetical host-observed intervals in seconds, not benchmark data.
from mlsysim import second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_qty, check

class ObservedCriticalPath:
    # 1. LOAD: one clock; parallel checks start together; no other dependencies.
    retrieval = (0.0, 0.2)
    planning = (0.2, 3.2)
    tests = (3.2, 9.2)
    lint = (3.2, 5.2)
    synthesis = (9.7, 11.7)
    segment = (0.0, 11.7)
    faster_test_s = 1.0  # intervention assumption, not an observed improvement

    # 2. EXECUTE: seconds throughout; enclosing span is not added to children.
    retrieval_s = retrieval[1] - retrieval[0]
    planning_s = planning[1] - planning[0]
    tests_s = tests[1] - tests[0]
    lint_s = lint[1] - lint[0]
    synthesis_s = synthesis[1] - synthesis[0]
    wall_s = segment[1] - segment[0]
    leaf_sum_s = retrieval_s + planning_s + tests_s + lint_s + synthesis_s
    accounted_s = retrieval_s + planning_s + max(tests_s, lint_s) + synthesis_s
    gap_s = synthesis[0] - max(tests[1], lint[1])
    changed_s = retrieval_s + planning_s + max(faster_test_s, lint_s) + gap_s + synthesis_s
    saving_s = wall_s - changed_s
    reduction_s = tests_s - faster_test_s

    # 3. GUARD: boundaries, overlap, and independent path enumeration.
    check(retrieval[1] == planning[0], "Serial retrieval-to-planning boundary")
    check(planning[1] == tests[0] == lint[0], "Checks start together")
    check(gap_s >= 0, "Synthesis follows both checks")
    check(abs(leaf_sum_s - 13.2) < 1e-9, "Overlapping leaf-duration sum")
    check(abs(accounted_s + gap_s - wall_s) < 1e-9, "Complete elapsed accounting")
    check(abs(wall_s - 11.7) < 1e-9 and abs(gap_s - 0.5) < 1e-9, "Declared observation window")
    check(abs(changed_s - max(0.2 + 3 + 1 + 0.5 + 2, 0.2 + 3 + 2 + 0.5 + 2)) < 1e-9, "Recompute both paths")
    check(abs(saving_s - 4.0) < 1e-9, "Saving limited by the other branch")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every export is consumed below.
    retrieval_interval_str = f"[{fmt_int(retrieval[0])}, {fmt(retrieval[1], precision=1)}]"
    planning_interval_str = f"[{fmt(planning[0], precision=1)}, {fmt(planning[1], precision=1)}]"
    tests_interval_str = f"[{fmt(tests[0], precision=1)}, {fmt(tests[1], precision=1)}]"
    lint_interval_str = f"[{fmt(lint[0], precision=1)}, {fmt(lint[1], precision=1)}]"
    synthesis_interval_str = f"[{fmt(synthesis[0], precision=1)}, {fmt(synthesis[1], precision=1)}]"
    wall_str = fmt_qty(wall_s * second, second, precision=1)
    leaf_sum_str = fmt_qty(leaf_sum_s * second, second, precision=1)
    accounted_str = fmt_qty(accounted_s * second, second, precision=1)
    gap_str = fmt_qty(gap_s * second, second, precision=1)
    faster_str = fmt_qty(faster_test_s * second, second, precision=0)
    changed_str = fmt_qty(changed_s * second, second, precision=1)
    saving_str = fmt_qty(saving_s * second, second, precision=0)
    reduction_str = fmt_qty(reduction_s * second, second, precision=0)
```

::: {#nbk-13-critical-path-latency-and-bottleneck .callout-notebook title="Observed time and the critical path"}

**Problem**: How much elapsed time do the recorded spans explain, and how much would shortening one check reduce the segment if the other durations and dependencies stayed unchanged?

**Assumptions**: @Tbl-vol3-trace-hierarchy gives observations from a separate hypothetical timing trial in an isolated environment, inspecting fixed candidate `ws_r19`. Its test operations carry new trial-specific identities. The model first proposes checks, the runtime admits two independent read-only checks with private scratch, and synthesis waits for both. All intervals use one host clock and include any wait inside the named client boundary. No hidden dependency delays either check's start, and admission takes no separate time. The enclosing segment runs from retrieval dispatch through the final response.

| Observed span                      | Interval after segment start (s)                       | Required predecessor                         |
|:-----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|
| Retrieve supporting context        | `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.retrieval_interval_str` | Segment start                                |
| Model call proposing checks        | `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.planning_interval_str`  | Retrieval response                           |
| Targeted tests                     | `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.tests_interval_str`     | Validated and admitted check proposal        |
| Static lint check                  | `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.lint_interval_str`      | Same proposal; independent of targeted tests |
| Model call synthesizing the report | `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.synthesis_interval_str` | Both check responses                         |

: **Hypothetical observed span intervals**: The two checks overlap. The enclosing segment measures `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.wall_str`; its duration is not additional work to sum with these children. {#tbl-vol3-trace-hierarchy}

**Math**: Adding all leaf durations gives `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.leaf_sum_str`, which exceeds elapsed time because it counts both concurrent checks. Retrieval, planning, the longer check, and synthesis instead account for `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.accounted_str`. The remaining `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.gap_str` lies between the last check response and synthesis. The capture leaves its cause unnamed, which is a reason for finer instrumentation rather than a finding about serialization or scheduling.

**Intervention**: Suppose a change reduced the targeted-test interval to `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.faster_str` without changing its coverage, either check's start, the lint duration, the gap, or the model calls. The lint check would become the limiting branch. Recomputing the graph gives `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.changed_str` for the segment, a saving of `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.saving_str`. Subtracting the entire reduction in test duration would incorrectly assume that the original critical path stayed critical.

**Systems insight**: A branch speedup is worth at most its slack over the next-longest parallel branch. Cutting the test by `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.reduction_str` saves only `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.saving_str` because lint then limits the path. Recompute the critical path before valuing any speedup, and treat the predicted saving as a hypothesis for a controlled trial, since a real change can also alter contention, coverage, and later model behavior.

:::

::: {#chk-13-trajectory-instrumentation .callout-checkpoint title="Interpret the trace's evidence"}

- [ ] **Identity**: Why does sharing a trace ID neither authorize a tool call nor make a result applicable to a different candidate revision?
- [ ] **Outcome**: A client span ends at timeout, and a later grader remains pending. Which operation and task conclusions are still unavailable?
- [ ] **Overlap**: Why do parent-child links and concurrent checks prevent summing every span duration into task latency?
- [ ] **Missing time**: What additional capture would be needed to explain the notebook's gap, and why does its location not identify a unique cause?
- [ ] **Changed path**: Using the notebook's intervals, how much would the segment shrink if the lint check, rather than the tests, were cut to `{python} ObservedCriticalPath.faster_str`? What does your answer imply about where to spend optimization effort?

:::

Tracing defines the evidence an investigator would like to inspect. Whether that evidence remains available depends on capture, sampling, retention, and access policy. The next section governs those choices, keeping recovery obligations intact and treating a missing diagnostic record as missing evidence.

## Trace Retention and Privacy {#sec-vol3-evaluation-budgets}

A trace can explain only what remains available to inspect. If the pending regression suite for `ws_r19` later fails, that trial becomes diagnostically important after its model and tool spans have ended. Retention therefore needs the task verdict and its timing, not just process exit codes or span status.

Retaining more content also increases storage, processing, and disclosure exposure. The design question is which evidence each purpose requires, how its inclusion is decided, and which conclusions remain possible when capture or access is limited.

### Separate accounting from diagnostic detail

Perspective \ref{psp-13-telemetry-duality} separated recovery history from diagnostic traces. Evaluation adds a third record, the accounting record, which identifies every admitted trial, its configuration and criteria, current verdict, measured costs, and unavailable evidence. The three can share storage or references, but sampling applies to diagnostic detail only, never to recovery history or the evaluation denominator.

The accounting record itself needs a capture and retention contract. Preserve the evaluated cohort, observation cutoff, criterion-level verdicts, and their sources. A lost registration or verdict update must appear as missing evidence. Otherwise an apparently complete denominator can omit precisely the difficult trials that finish late or fail to report.

Diagnostic detail also grows faster than the trajectory when spans mirror content. If each model-call span copies the full delivered history, trace volume inherits the quadratic resend growth of @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend. Referencing unchanged history by digest and storing each new observation once keeps volume linear in turns, provided the referenced bytes remain retained.

**Head sampling**\index{Head sampling!definition} selects detailed traces near the start of execution. A random sample with known inclusion probabilities can support population estimates under the sampling and capture assumptions. Its weakness for diagnosis is that a rare failure may have no retained detailed example.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-head-sampling-miss
#| echo: false
# RARE FAILURES UNDER HEAD SAMPLING (LEGO)
# Goal: Probability that a failure mode leaves no detailed trace.
# Scope: Independent retention with fixed probability, decided before outcomes.
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_percent, check

class HeadSamplingMiss:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical head-sampling probability and occurrence counts.
    theta = 0.10
    rare_count = 5
    common_count = 50
    chk_theta, chk_count = 0.05, 20  # checkpoint exercise givens

    # 2. EXECUTE: each occurrence retained independently with probability theta.
    miss_rare = (1 - theta) ** rare_count
    miss_common = (1 - theta) ** common_count

    # 3. GUARD
    check(abs(miss_rare - 0.59049) < 1e-9, "Five occurrences, ten percent")
    check(miss_common < 0.01, "Fifty occurrences")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    theta_str = fmt_percent(theta, precision=0, style="prose")
    rare_count_str = fmt_int(rare_count)
    common_count_str = fmt_int(common_count)
    chk_theta_str = fmt_percent(chk_theta, precision=0, style="prose")
    chk_count_str = fmt_int(chk_count)
    miss_rare_str = fmt_percent(round(miss_rare, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    miss_common_str = fmt_percent(round(miss_common, 3), precision=1, style="prose")
```

The loss is easy to quantify. Head sampling decides before the outcome is known, so each occurrence of a failure mode is retained independently with the sampling probability $\theta$, and a mode that occurs $n_f$ times leaves no detailed trace with probability $(1-\theta)^{n_f}$. At $\theta$ equal to `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.theta_str`, a failure mode seen `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.rare_count_str` times has about a `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.miss_rare_str` chance of leaving no detailed example; at `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.common_count_str` occurrences that chance falls to `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.miss_common_str`. Rare failure modes are exactly the ones a uniform sample is least likely to retain. **Tail sampling**\index{Tail sampling!definition} selects using evidence accumulated later, such as a failed acceptance check or an unusually costly run. It concentrates diagnostic storage on important cases, and the resulting collection is deliberately unrepresentative of ordinary traffic.

The population failure rate therefore comes from the complete accounting record, never from the tail-selected traces. When estimating from sampled records, preserve inclusion probabilities, selection-policy versions, and relevant strata; weighting requires an appropriate sampling design and nonzero inclusion for the cases being estimated. Retain a known sample of ordinary accepted trials as controls, since a failure trace alone cannot show which behavior is unusual.

### Make the verdict window explicit

Tail selection can span more than one decision. Specify an initial decision boundary, a window for later verdicts, and the update policy. A trace can be provisionally retained while acceptance is pending, then assigned its final retention class when evidence arrives. If the detailed body has already expired, a late failure can update the accounting record but cannot recover the discarded bytes. Record that gap and the verdict delay.

@Tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies illustrates a policy structure rather than universal retention rates. Categories can overlap; apply a declared precedence or deduplicate selections so one trace is not counted several times.

| Evidence at the decision boundary                                | Possible detailed-trace policy                                           | Limit to record                                                                                  |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Failed task criterion or enforced-policy violation               | Give high retention priority, with the criterion and supporting evidence | A process error alone does not establish whole-task failure; priority does not guarantee capture |
| Pending or unknown task verdict                                  | Retain provisionally or under an explicit unresolved-case sample         | State the deadline, missing evidence, and what happens when the window expires                   |
| Accepted but unusually slow, costly, or intervention-heavy trial | Retain under declared diagnostic thresholds                              | Selection enriches those behaviors and does not establish their population frequency             |
| Ordinary accepted trial                                          | Retain a known random control sample                                     | Preserve its inclusion probability and distinguish unsampled from lost                           |

: **Verdict-aware trace selection**: Selection uses the declared task criteria and available evidence, including delayed outcomes. Trace completion is not equivalent to task acceptance. {#tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies}

::: {.column-margin}
**Eviction priority.** Under buffer pressure, drop routine-success and unclassified traces before traces flagged by a failed criterion or policy violation. Priority reduces the loss of diagnostic evidence; it does not guarantee retention.
:::

Finite buffers limit this policy. Bound live trace count, aggregate retained bytes, individual trace size, and waiting age. Mean live count times mean trace size is a planning estimate that a burst of long, large traces can exceed. Reserved high-priority capacity reduces losses, and spilling to an authorized durable store moves the capacity limit rather than removing it.

Expose truncation, eviction, dropped records, and unavailable intervals. Monitor them by the relevant cohort and selection class, since correlated loss during incidents can remove precisely the traces most needed for diagnosis. Selection after collection can reduce downstream storage and export without reducing the bytes initially received, processed, or buffered. Privacy restrictions apply to those earlier copies too. @Fig-vol3-tail-sampling-pipeline places the capture boundary, the buffer, verdict-aware selection, and the accounting record on one path.

::: {#fig-vol3-tail-sampling-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Verdict-Aware Trace Selection**: Trace bodies pass a fallible minimization boundary into a bounded buffer that holds them until task verdicts, which can arrive late, reach the selector. Selection applies a declared precedence among the classes of @tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies, keeps inclusion probabilities with retained traces, and discards unselected bodies. Every admitted trial also enters the accounting record directly, together with recorded drops, evictions, and truncation, so the denominator does not depend on which bodies survived. Priority raises the chance that a failure's detail is kept; it does not guarantee retention." fig-alt="Left-to-right flow diagram. An admitted-trials box feeds a capture boundary box labeled minimize, redact, fallible, which feeds a bounded buffer labeled held until the verdict window, evicts lowest priority first. The buffer feeds a verdict-aware selection box that also receives task verdicts, which can arrive late, from above. The selection box lists four numbered classes: failed criterion or violation, high priority, not guaranteed; pending or unknown, provisional until its deadline; accepted but slow or costly, declared diagnostic thresholds; and ordinary accepted, random control sample. Arrows lead from selection to a detailed trace store that keeps inclusion probability and to a discarded box for unselected bodies. Along the bottom, an evaluation accounting record receives an arrow from admitted trials labeled every trial and a dashed red arrow from the buffer labeled drops, evictions, truncation."}
![](images/svg/tail-sampling-pipeline.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: lego-13-telemetry-ingestion-inverted-economics
#| echo: false
# VERDICT-AWARE RETAINED VOLUME (LEGO)
# Goal: Compare expected downstream diagnostic bytes under two selections.
# Scope: Hypothetical disjoint classes, equal trace sizes, no capture loss.
from mlsysim import Q_
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_memory, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, check

class TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics:
    # 1. LOAD: one hourly cohort, not measured workload characteristics.
    trials = 10_000
    failed = 400
    unresolved = 100
    ordinary = 9_500
    trace_size = Q_(1.4, "megabyte")  # decimal MB, complete permitted body
    hours = 24
    head_probability = 0.05
    control_probability = 0.02
    control_step = 0.01  # one percentage point of control sampling

    # 2. EXECUTE: high-priority classes all fit in the assumed window.
    head_count = trials * head_probability
    head_failed = failed * head_probability
    head_unresolved = unresolved * head_probability
    tail_ordinary = ordinary * control_probability
    tail_count = failed + unresolved + tail_ordinary
    full_volume = trials * hours * trace_size
    head_volume = head_count * hours * trace_size
    tail_volume = tail_count * hours * trace_size
    ratio = (full_volume / tail_volume).to("").magnitude
    floor_volume = (failed + unresolved) * hours * trace_size
    per_point_volume = ordinary * control_step * hours * trace_size

    # 3. GUARD: conservation and independently stated byte totals.
    check(failed + unresolved + ordinary == trials, "Disjoint complete cohort")
    check(head_count == 500 and tail_count == 690, "Expected selected traces")
    check((head_failed, head_unresolved, tail_ordinary) == (20, 5, 190), "Expected selected classes")
    check(abs(full_volume.to("gigabyte").magnitude - 336) < 1e-9, "Full daily decimal GB")
    check(abs(head_volume.to("gigabyte").magnitude - 16.8) < 1e-9, "Head daily decimal GB")
    check(abs(tail_volume.to("gigabyte").magnitude - 23.184) < 1e-9, "Tail daily decimal GB")

    # 4. OUTPUT: every formatted export is consumed below.
    trials_str = fmt_int(trials)
    failed_str = fmt_int(failed)
    unresolved_str = fmt_int(unresolved)
    ordinary_str = fmt_int(ordinary)
    trace_mb_str = fmt_memory(trace_size, unit="MB", precision=1)
    hours_str = fmt_int(hours)
    head_probability_str = fmt_percent(head_probability, precision=0, style="prose")
    control_probability_str = fmt_percent(control_probability, precision=0, style="prose")
    head_failed_str = fmt_int(head_failed)
    head_unresolved_str = fmt_int(head_unresolved)
    tail_ordinary_str = fmt_int(tail_ordinary)
    head_count_str = fmt_int(head_count)
    tail_count_str = fmt_int(tail_count)
    full_gb_str = fmt_memory(full_volume, unit="GB", precision=0)
    head_gb_str = fmt_memory(head_volume, unit="GB", precision=1)
    tail_gb_str = fmt_memory(tail_volume, unit="GB", precision=3)
    reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio, precision=1)
    floor_gb_str = fmt_memory(floor_volume, unit="GB", precision=1)
    per_point_gb_str = fmt_memory(per_point_volume, unit="GB", precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-13-telemetry-ingestion-inverted-economics .callout-notebook title="What verdict-aware selection saves"}

**Problem**: How much downstream diagnostic storage do uniform head sampling and verdict-aware tail selection use for the same hypothetical workload?

**Assumptions**: Each hour brings `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.trials_str` trials with equal `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.trace_mb_str` permitted trace bodies. At the selection boundary, `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.failed_str` have failed criteria, `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.unresolved_str` remain pending or unknown, and `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.ordinary_str` are ordinary accepted trials. These classes are disjoint and repeat for `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.hours_str` hours. All bodies fit the capture window and survive collection; there are no additional promotions or outlier classes. Head selection samples each trial with probability `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.head_probability_str`. Tail selection retains the failed and unresolved classes and independently samples `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.control_probability_str` of ordinary accepted trials.

**Math**: Keeping every body requires `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.full_gb_str` over the stated period. Head sampling retains an expected `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.head_count_str` traces/hour, or `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.head_gb_str` over the stated period. It includes an expected `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.head_failed_str` failed and `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.head_unresolved_str` unresolved trials per hour, not guaranteed counts. Tail selection retains `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.failed_str` failed, `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.unresolved_str` unresolved, and an expected `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.tail_ordinary_str` ordinary accepted trials: `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.tail_count_str` traces/hour and `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.tail_gb_str` over the stated period.

**Result**: Full retention uses about `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.reduction_mult_str` the downstream bytes of the tail policy. Tail selection spends more than head selection to keep every failed and unresolved trial rather than an expected handful per hour.

**Systems insight**: Retained volume is a floor set by the failure-plus-unresolved fraction, `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.floor_gb_str` per day here, plus a term set by the control rate on ordinary traffic, where each percentage point of control sampling adds `{python} TelemetryIngestionInvertedEconomics.per_point_gb_str` per day. Storage planning therefore tunes the control rate and budgets the floor to grow in proportion to the failure rate. Volumes are decimal and exclude indexing, replication, accounting records, and recovery history, and preselection ingestion is unchanged.

:::

### Minimize disclosure before export

The permitted trace body is itself a design choice. Start with the fields required for the investigation: typed outcomes, versions, timing, selection decisions, and protected artifact references may suffice without copying whole prompts or tool replies. Tool arguments can contain private fixture information even when they contain no credentials. Trace identifiers, filenames, and pseudonyms can also reveal relationships. Authorization must cover the content and recipient, not merely an approved telemetry service name.

Apply minimization at the trusted capture boundary before content reaches an unauthorized collector, queue, or alert. Protect authorized local buffers and intermediate copies as well as the final store. Use access scope, retention periods, and deletion handling appropriate to each record class, including derived indexes and known downstream copies. Required recovery evidence needs an explicitly authorized storage policy; labeling it diagnostic does not excuse its loss or authorize unrestricted retention.

Redaction reduces exposure and is fallible. Pattern matching can miss unfamiliar secrets; entropy tests can flag benign identifiers while missing predictable credentials; entity recognizers can omit private information or remove useful evidence. Because no combination of them certifies an arbitrary payload, prefer excluding unnecessary fields and validating structured output, then test remaining transformations on representative sensitive cases and record their versions and limitations.

Where correlation is necessary, keyed pseudonyms can replace selected identifiers. An HMAC uses a secret key, not a public salt, as specified in [RFC 2104](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104.html#section-2). Stable pseudonyms retain linkability, and auxiliary information or access to a matching service can still reveal identity. Scope keys and access to the intended tenant and correlation domain; rotation limits cross-period linkage but also interrupts longitudinal analysis. Truncation trades space for collision risk. Pseudonymization is neither anonymization nor permission to retain the underlying information indefinitely.

### State the remaining replay fidelity

Redaction can change the evidence needed for diagnosis. Removing a fixture value may hide why a test failed; replacing text can change parsing or a model's next proposal. A sanitized trace therefore cannot automatically substitute for the bytes actually delivered during the historical execution.

When exact captured inputs are necessary and retention is authorized, keep them in a separately protected artifact store and expose scoped references in the diagnostic record. Preserve which transformation produced the diagnostic view. If exact artifacts are unavailable, expired, or inaccessible to the investigator, state the narrower comparison that remains possible. A compatible synthetic fixture can support a new experiment, not a claim to have reproduced the original input.

::: {.callout-checkpoint title="Retained evidence and supported conclusions"}

- [ ] **Buffer expiration**: A broader acceptance check fails after the trace buffer expires. What can the accounting record establish, and what can it no longer provide for diagnosis?
- [ ] **Tail-sampling bias**: Why does the failure fraction in a tail-selected collection not estimate the population failure rate without an appropriate inclusion design?
- [ ] **Head-sampling estimate**: Uniform head sampling keeps `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.chk_theta_str` of traces, and a failure mode has occurred `{python} HeadSamplingMiss.chk_count_str` times. Estimate the chance that no detailed trace of it survives, and decide whether verdict-aware selection is worth its extra storage for this mode.
- [ ] **Sanitized replay**: A sanitized observation is available but its original protected artifact has expired. Which replay claim must be narrowed, and why is its digest insufficient?

:::

Retention determines which observations survive; privacy policy determines which of them an investigator may use. A postmortem must begin with those boundaries. The next section distinguishes reconstruction, captured-input regression, and new experiments so that each diagnostic result claims only what the retained record supports.

## Incident Postmortems {#sec-vol3-evaluation-postmortems}

Suppose a trial of the connection-pool repair fails after receiving a silently truncated search result. The retained response ends in the middle of a source excerpt, and the next model response proposes replacing a file outside the permitted repair scope. The runtime rejects that proposal before dispatch. The trace locates the observation and the refusal; whether a corrected observation would have produced an accepted repair is a separate question. An incident postmortem connects such evidence to a testable explanation and a scoped corrective change.

The investigation must keep its initial findings separate. A delivered excerpt that omitted required truncation metadata can establish an interface defect. A forbidden proposal establishes behavior by the model, while the admission record establishes whether the runtime blocked it. Had an unauthorized write executed, enforcement would need its own investigation, whatever the observation said. Several components can contribute to the same rejected task. Assigning one subsystem label too early hides the conditions that a repair must address.

### Reconstruct before experimenting {#sec-vol3-postmortem-replay}

The three modes in @sec-vol3-persistence-replay answer different questions. Reconstructing a recorded projection folds retained decisions with the compatible checkpoint. Harness regression replay instead exercises code against captured inputs with live effects disabled. A counterfactual branch changes a declared condition and obtains observations valid for the new path. Only the first reconstructs the selected historical state; neither of the other modes supplies a missing historical outcome.

For the earlier crash, folding `record_R_C` and its compatible suffix still leaves `test_r18`, attempt `attempt1`, unresolved if no settling evidence survives. A newly successful test does not fill that historical gap. The evaluation trial has its own identity, configuration, and candidate artifacts, so its diagnostic branches must remain distinct from both the original operation and the worked trial's `ws_r19`.

Historical inspection begins with what is available under the capture and retention contract. The delivered context can show the excerpt the model received; separately retained raw output can show what the adapter omitted. Byte-exact comparison needs the retained bytes themselves, while redacted observations support inspection of status and structure. The separation between recovery history and diagnostic capture in perspective \ref{psp-13-telemetry-duality} therefore bounds what the postmortem can claim.

Regression replay can isolate a transformation without making a fresh model call. Supply the captured tool response to the old and revised observation adapters and compare their delivered envelopes against the stated output contract. Keep production dispatch, background reconciliation, and other live effect paths disabled. This test can establish that the old adapter omitted a required partial-result marker and that the revised adapter supplies it for this input. It cannot establish how a model will respond to the revised envelope.

That latter question requires a new experiment. Changing temperature, prompt text, model configuration, or the observation rule is an intervention, even when the engineer calls it replay. Preserve the declared unchanged settings and record available model provenance; a seed alone does not fix every service input. As with the recorded-response fixtures of @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms, recorded downstream responses remain reusable only while the operation, relevant arguments, candidate, versions, and ordering assumptions match. Matching only the tool name can manufacture a successful continuation by giving the new action evidence that belongs to the old one.

### Turn a localized defect into a hypothesis {#sec-vol3-postmortem-attribution}

The first observed mismatch narrows an investigation to a hypothesis. In the repair example, inspecting the raw search result and delivered envelope can localize silent truncation to the observation adapter. The hypothesis is that the missing completeness signal contributes to inappropriate repair proposals. Testing that hypothesis requires an outcome measured after the intervention, rather than another reading of the same trace.

@Tbl-vol3-fault-attribution distinguishes useful evidence from the claim it cannot support alone. The rows are investigation paths that can overlap, not mutually exclusive diagnoses.

| Suspected boundary    | Evidence or controlled comparison                                           | Limit of the finding                                                                 |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Context assembly      | Compare retained source versions, delivered messages, and omission metadata | An omitted fact is not proof that restoring it will complete the task                |
| Tool observation      | Compare captured output with the adapter's declared and delivered envelopes | A truncation defect does not make the model's later inference correct                |
| Model response        | Repeat the specified invocation or continuation under controlled conditions | A different response does not identify temperature or sampling as the original cause |
| Runtime admission     | Exercise captured proposals and control inputs against the stated guards    | A rejected proposal differs from an unauthorized operation that was dispatched       |
| Execution environment | Compare endpoint evidence, configuration, and relevant fault records        | A timeout or process termination signal alone does not identify its underlying cause |

: **Evidence for diagnostic hypotheses**: Localization constrains an explanation without making the subsystem categories exclusive. {#tbl-vol3-fault-attribution}

For example, a process killed by a signal may have exceeded a memory limit, received an administrative termination request, or encountered another termination path. The signal alone does not distinguish those cases. Likewise, a schema-valid model response may still rely on an unsupported assumption. The investigation needs the relevant runtime or environment evidence before choosing a correction. A model's explanation of its own response is a hypothesis to test, not evidence for it.

### Test a controlled change {#sec-vol3-postmortem-ablation}

A controlled diagnostic experiment states the starting boundary, intervention, unchanged configuration, permitted randomness, and common outcomes before comparing runs. The starting fixture includes the candidate and any environment state needed by that boundary. Resetting only the files while changing the service behavior would introduce another factor. Randomized or interleaved execution helps separate an intervention from drift in shared services; any remaining interference belongs in the limitations.

An observation-contract change can combine several mechanisms. Adding a partial-result marker and enabling continuation reads tests that package, not the marker alone. To distinguish the contribution of the marker from access to the missing content, the engineer needs further conditions that vary those features separately. Effects can also depend on the model or task. The [NIST discussion of one-factor experiments](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pri/section2/pri212.htm) explains why changing one factor while holding others fixed does not reveal their interactions.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-evaluation-diagnostic-counts
#| echo: false
# DIAGNOSTIC EXPERIMENT COUNTS AND WHAT A CLEAN RUN BOUNDS (LEGO)
# Goal: Stipulated branch outcomes; Wilson upper failure bound after all-accepted runs.
# Scope: Hypothetical continuations from one saved prefix; not a task-population sample.
from math import ceil
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_percent, check

class DiagnosticCounts:
    # 1. LOAD: stipulated outcomes per condition, and a checkpoint target bound.
    runs = 20
    original_accepted = 1
    warning_accepted = 8
    revised_accepted = 20
    target_bound = 0.05  # checkpoint exercise: failure-rate bound to demonstrate
    z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)

    # 2. EXECUTE: Wilson upper limit on failure after zero observed failures.
    revised_fail_upper = z * z / (runs + z * z)
    runs_for_target = ceil(z * z * (1 - target_bound) / target_bound)

    # 3. GUARD
    check(revised_accepted == runs, "Revised condition accepts every run")
    check(0 <= original_accepted < warning_accepted < runs, "Stipulated ordering")
    check(0.15 < revised_fail_upper < 0.17, "Twenty clean runs bound failure near sixteen percent")
    check(runs_for_target > 3 * runs, "Target bound needs far more runs")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    runs_str = fmt_int(runs)
    original_accepted_str = fmt_int(original_accepted)
    original_rejected_str = fmt_int(runs - original_accepted)
    warning_accepted_str = fmt_int(warning_accepted)
    warning_stopped_str = fmt_int(runs - warning_accepted)
    revised_accepted_str = fmt_int(revised_accepted)
    revised_fail_upper_str = fmt_percent(round(revised_fail_upper, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    target_bound_str = fmt_percent(target_bound, precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#exmp-13-counterfactual-ablation-of-a-silent .callout-example title="A controlled test of observation completeness"}

**Problem**: A diagnostic fixture reproduces a silently truncated search result during the connection-pool repair. What do the following hypothetical outcomes support about a proposed interface change?

**Scenario**: Experiment `diag_pool_truncation_v1` uses a compatible saved prefix of task `pool_repair_01` in `pool_fixture_v1`. It restores a private copy for every continuation. The branch identities distinguish the original interface, an added warning, and a revised paginated interface; each run also records its own candidate artifact and operation identities. These branches do not overwrite `ws_r18`, relabel `ws_r19`, or settle the old `test_r18` request.

All conditions use the same model configuration, sampling settings, starting candidate, permitted operations, budget policy, and checks. Each receives `{python} DiagnosticCounts.runs_str` fresh stochastic continuations. Acceptance uses the repair's required artifact checks and other criteria, with the diagnostic protocol explicitly rejecting a run that proposes the out-of-scope rewrite. The unchanged admission gate blocks such proposals before dispatch. A denial therefore records a forbidden proposal without recording an executed unauthorized write. Every run reaches a known assessment in this stipulated example; an unavailable assessment would remain a separate outcome.

The original-interface condition deliberately retains the adapter defect, delivering the truncated excerpt without an omission notice. Its stipulated outcomes are `{python} DiagnosticCounts.original_accepted_str` accepted repair and `{python} DiagnosticCounts.original_rejected_str` rejected runs that propose the forbidden rewrite. A warning-only condition adds an instruction that search results may be incomplete, but provides no reliable continuation mechanism. Its outcomes are `{python} DiagnosticCounts.warning_accepted_str` accepted repairs and `{python} DiagnosticCounts.warning_stopped_str` budget-limited runs without an accepted repair; none proposes the forbidden rewrite. The revised-interface condition supplies typed partial-result metadata and a supported way to retrieve remaining results. Its outcomes are `{python} DiagnosticCounts.revised_accepted_str` accepted repairs and no nonaccepted runs, with no forbidden rewrite proposal. No condition dispatches an unauthorized write.

**Diagnosis**: Avoiding the forbidden proposal and completing the repair are different outcomes. The warning-only runs illustrate the distinction: the inappropriate proposal disappears, but some continuations still stop without acceptance. The paginated-interface results support testing that intervention package more broadly. They do not show that the marker alone produced the improvement, that the model made a rational deduction from the damaged excerpt, or that model behavior played no part in the failure.

The fresh runs estimate behavior conditional on this saved prefix and fixture. Even `{python} DiagnosticCounts.revised_accepted_str` accepted runs out of `{python} DiagnosticCounts.runs_str` leave the Wilson upper limit of @sec-vol3-evaluation-wilson on the revised condition's failure rate at `{python} DiagnosticCounts.revised_fail_upper_str`. The counts also stay out of the separate task-set comparison, where pooling them would inflate the release sample.

**Systems insight**: The observation boundary has a directly testable defect, and the stipulated continuation outcomes make its repair worth evaluating. Preserve the admission guard in every condition, measure task acceptance separately from rejected proposals and executed effects, and test the revised system on additional held-out tasks before making a release claim.

:::

The example follows the bounded-observation contract from @sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming. Pagination must have a real retrieval contract tied to the intended source version, and each additional read consumes its declared resources. A marker that advertises unavailable content would introduce another interface defect.

### Preserve a scoped regression

A corrective change needs tests at the boundary it repairs and at the task outcome it is intended to improve. For the adapter, deterministic tests can supply complete, partial, malformed, and unavailable outputs and check the represented status, omission metadata, and valid continuation behavior. Tests of the admission gate supply the out-of-scope proposal directly and verify that no dispatch occurs under the declared policy. These tests do not need the model to generate the failure again.

End-to-end tests add a different obligation. Run the revised agent in the isolated fixture and inspect the resulting candidate, required checks, process constraints, costs, and residual duties. A runtime `COMPLETED` label alone is insufficient. The final artifact must satisfy the evaluation criteria for its own revision, while environment release and unresolved operations retain the handling required by the task contract. Repeat stochastic tests under a declared comparison protocol; a passing regression case is one sample, not a bound on recurrence.

The investigation record in @tbl-vol3-postmortem-template preserves the boundary between established defect, tested intervention, and remaining uncertainty. A real report links actual versions and evidence.

| Report element          | Evidence to preserve                                                                                                      |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Incident and coverage   | Task, trial, configuration, candidate, relevant operation identities, retained interval, and missing or redacted material |
| Established findings    | Delivered partial observation without required metadata; exact forbidden proposal and recorded pre-dispatch refusal       |
| Tested change           | Interface revision, compatible fixture and saved boundary, branch identities, unchanged guards, and allowed randomness    |
| Outcomes                | Common acceptance and proposal/effect criteria, every run's verdict, budget stops, and unavailable assessments            |
| Corrective verification | Adapter and admission tests, repeated task-level checks, and the actual revision tested                                   |
| Remaining questions     | Untested fixtures and interactions, retention limits, residual-operation owners, and evidence needed for release          |

: **A bounded postmortem record**: The report records what supports a correction and what still requires evaluation; it is not a certificate of an exclusive cause. {#tbl-vol3-postmortem-template}

::: {#chk-13-fleet-sre-metrics .callout-checkpoint title="Diagnosis and regression scope"}

Use the repair experiment to distinguish a localized defect from a release claim.

- [ ] **Replay modes**: Which test can establish that an adapter omitted a required marker without making a fresh model call, and what can that test not establish?
- [ ] **Changed requests**: Why must a branch requesting another page obtain a matching observation instead of consuming the next recorded tool result?
- [ ] **Common outcomes**: Why do fewer forbidden proposals not necessarily imply more accepted repairs?
- [ ] **Diagnostic sample size**: About how many consecutive accepted continuations would the revised interface need before the Wilson upper limit on its failure rate fell below `{python} DiagnosticCounts.target_bound_str`?
- [ ] **Regression scope**: Which checks test the adapter, which test admission, and which test completion of the repaired task?

:::

A postmortem can produce an established interface defect, a tested correction, and a regression fixture while leaving broader reliability uncertain. That is enough to justify a candidate change, not unrestricted deployment. Staged release evaluation determines which additional tasks and operating conditions the candidate may encounter while collecting the next evidence.

## Staged Releases {#sec-vol3-evaluation-releases}

In the hypothetical diagnostic experiment, the revised observation interface produced accepted repairs on the isolated fixture. That result supports testing the change on a broader task set, and production authority is a separate grant. A release decision must connect the proposed change to its evaluation evidence and to the consequences of being wrong. For an agent, those consequences include operations and charges that can remain outstanding after new traffic stops.

Staging separates the evidence available before live execution from evidence that requires it. Offline trials compare configurations on declared fixtures. **Shadow execution**\index{Shadow execution!definition} tests a candidate against authorized copies of current inputs without assigning it the live task. A **canary**\index{Canary release!definition} assigns a bounded portion of eligible live tasks to a candidate under an explicit release policy. Each stage keeps the task's existing grant and answers its own question, so success in one leaves the next stage's conditions open. Causal and statistical release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}) supports a scoped decision at each step. @Fig-vol3-canary-deployment-pipeline lays out the stages and the hold that any of them can trigger.

::: {#fig-vol3-canary-deployment-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Staged Release and Its Hold Path**: Each stage applies its own criterion: the paired lower bound $L_\Delta$ against the declared margin offline, tool-call drift $D_{\mathrm{JS}}$ in shadow execution, and the sequential statistic $\Lambda_n$ with hard tripwires in the canary. A wider release requires every criterion of the gate $G$ in @eq-vol3-eval-release-gate. An unmet or inconclusive offline result, a drift review that finds a problem, or a canary alarm leads to the same hold. The hold stops new candidate admission; outstanding candidate operations keep their identities and owners, and recovery, not rollback, settles their effects." fig-alt="Four stage cards in a row joined by arrows labeled met. Stage 1, offline comparison: paired tasks with declared fixtures and matched criteria, a gate box reading L sub delta greater than minus delta sub tol, and a note that inconclusive counts as not met. Stage 2, shadow execution: authorized copy of live inputs with output withheld, a gate box reading D sub JS of P sub b and P sub c for tool-call drift, and a note that difference is not regression. Stage 3, canary: allocation rho of eligible live tasks with assignment sticky per trajectory, a gate box reading Lambda sub n versus ell and u, and a red hard tripwires badge for forbidden dispatch and exhausted limits. Stage 4, release decision: G equals 1 across paired margin, Theta, p99, and V sub c equals 0. Red arrows from stages 1, 2, and 3, labeled not met, review finds a problem, and alarm or tripwire, lead down to a hold band with two boxes: stop new candidate admission, and outstanding candidate work keeps its identities and owners while recovery settles effects and rollback does not undo them."}
![](images/svg/vol3-canary-deployment-pipeline.svg)
:::

### Separate offline comparison from shadow evidence

The offline decision uses the paired comparison from @sec-vol3-evaluation-paired, with the same acceptance criteria, sampling unit, budgets, and predeclared margin. A bound on the candidate-minus-baseline difference answers that comparison; comparing separate Wilson lower bounds does not. In the worked paired case, the lower difference bound does not meet the declared tolerance. The candidate therefore stays offline. Planned further evaluation or authorized diagnosis can proceed under a preplanned analysis, and favorable traces leave the unmet gate unmet.

For a configuration eligible for shadow evaluation, the input copy creates a separate execution with its own identity and allowance. The baseline still serves each original live task. Mirroring adds candidate executions on top of the baseline's traffic. Privacy and authorization checks must permit the copied input, its destinations, and the shadow tool operations. A request containing private fixture information cannot be sent to a new service merely because its output will be discarded.

The shadow environment determines which questions can be answered. An isolated stateful replica can support checks of the candidate's resulting artifact or simulated environment. A recorded-response fixture can support a narrower comparison while requests continue to match its assumptions. A synthetic success reply to an unperformed mutation does not establish that the mutation would work in production. @Tbl-vol3-dark-traffic-routing distinguishes the live task from the additional experiment.

| Boundary             | Baseline execution                                     | Shadow execution                                                                        |
|:---------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task assignment      | Serves the original admitted live task                 | Receives an authorized copy as a separate experiment                                    |
| Effects              | Uses only the live task's current grant                | Uses separately bounded isolated state or an explicitly supported observation path      |
| Data access          | Follows the task's disclosure and access policy        | Copying inputs and forwarding tool arguments require their own permitted recipients     |
| Acceptance evidence  | Applies the live task criteria                         | Applies only criteria supported by the shadow fixture's fidelity                        |
| Delivery and cleanup | Returns the task result through its authorized channel | Withholds candidate output from the live task and settles its own resources and charges |

: **Shadow execution boundaries**: Input mirroring adds an experiment. It neither divides the baseline's original task assignment nor makes the copied data and tool traffic harmless. {#tbl-vol3-dark-traffic-routing}

Read access still has effects. Queries can acquire locks, consume quotas, trigger logging, or disclose arguments; a shared replica can also expose other work to load. The shadow design must specify which services it contacts and what those contacts can do. Isolation and tool mediation from @sec-vol3-sandboxes and @sec-vol3-tool-calling supply the controls, while evaluation states which production behaviors the resulting fixture omits.

Tool selection, token use, and latency differences can expose a changed operating pattern before live task assignment. For tool selection, the Jensen–Shannon divergence [@lin1991divergence] between the baseline and candidate distributions of tool calls, $P_b$ and $P_c$, summarizes the change in one number:

$$D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P_b\,\|\,P_c)=\tfrac12 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_b\,\|\,M)+\tfrac12 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_c\,\|\,M),\qquad M=\tfrac12(P_b+P_c).$$ {#eq-vol3-eval-tool-drift}

Unlike the Kullback–Leibler divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$, it is symmetric and stays finite when one configuration uses a tool the other never calls; with natural logarithms, $0\le D_{\mathrm{JS}}\le\ln 2$, which gives a fixed scale for comparing releases. The distributions must come from comparable inputs and one declared action-counting policy. Difference alone is not regression. The intended repair may remove redundant calls. Compare the changed behavior with task acceptance, process constraints, and costs under comparable inputs. A shadow result can justify another test or a hold; it cannot supply evidence for production effects that the shadow deliberately prevented.
